title: LLM pretraining
lead: Everything between a pile of text and a base model: the compute budget, the data pipeline, the architecture and optimiser settings that hold at scale, the memory and parallelism arithmetic that decides what fits where, what breaks in a long run, and the two cheaper relatives an organisation actually runs, mid-training and continued pretraining. You work out on paper how a 9.5B-parameter base like the case study's is made and what continuing its pretraining would cost, then build a deduplication pass and pretrain, destabilise and adapt small GPTs on your own laptop.
prerequisites: Module 02: backpropagation, AdamW and learning-rate schedules, normalisation, debugging a training run
Module 06: the modern decoder block (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE, GQA, FlashAttention), parameter and FLOP counting (the FLOP rule this module applies), the tiny-GPT training loop

Module 07: the language-modelling objective and perplexity, BPE tokenisation, the Chinchilla scaling law L(N, D) with its compute-optimal allocation and the over-training argument, and the running case study
Module 05 (Section on mixture of experts) for the MoE concept; this module covers MoE engineering at scale
Probability: expectation, variance, independence and the binomial distribution (for MinHash, LSH and benchmark noise)
Comfort with orders of magnitude and units: FLOPs, FLOP/s, bytes, GB, GB/s
outcomes: Compute the training FLOPs, GPU-hours and calendar time of a run from its configuration, D, hardware peak and MFU with the series' FLOP rule (6ND without the input embedding, plus causal attention), and say how far the shortcut 6ND is off and why.
Use the Chinchilla fit to compare a compute-optimal and an over-trained run, including the number of served tokens at which over-training pays for itself and who pays it back.

Design a web-scale data pipeline (extraction, language ID, heuristic and model-based quality filters, PII handling, deduplication, decontamination, mixture, tokenizer, packing) and justify the order of its stages.
Implement MinHash with LSH banding, derive the candidate probability 1 - (1 - s^r)^b, and choose b and r for a target similarity threshold.
Size a decoder (layers, width, heads, FFN width, vocabulary) to a parameter budget, and state what changes in memory, compute and communication when its FFNs become a mixture of experts.
Set AdamW, the learning-rate schedule, batch size, gradient clipping, z-loss, QK-norm and numerical precision for a run, naming the failure each one prevents.

Compute per-GPU memory for weights, gradients, optimiser states, activations and logits under data parallelism and ZeRO stages 1-3, with and without activation checkpointing, and choose a parallel layout (FSDP/HSDP, tensor, pipeline, context) for a given cluster.
Diagnose a loss spike, a divergence, a data-loader bug or a hardware fault from training logs, and set a checkpoint interval from a failure rate.
Decide whether a team should continue pretraining an open base on its domain: measure the gap first, cost the run, and fix the go/no-go rule before spending.
Pretrain a 5.8M-parameter GPT on a laptop with a complete pipeline and logging, and continue a small base's pretraining on a domain corpus, measuring forgetting with and without replay.
software: PyTorch 2.x (CPU is enough; a GPU through Google Colab is optional and only speeds up Labs 2, 3 and 5)
pandas with pyarrow (to read one parquet file)
Hugging Face huggingface_hub (one 10 MB dataset download, shared by Labs 1, 2, 3 and 5) and tokenizers (BPE training)

sections.title: What pretraining is, and the budget first
sections.purpose: Define a pretraining run as one objective pursued under a compute budget fixed in advance, apply the series' FLOP rule to turn a budget into GPU-hours and calendar days, and make the compute decision for how a base like the case study's is made.
must_cover: The objective $\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{\text{docs}}\sum_t \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})$ over packed token sequences (perplexity and the objective's meaning are Module 07's; one-paragraph reminder and link). No labels, no tasks, no instructions; the result is a model of text, not an assistant, which Module 09 turns into one.

Why the decisions come first: a run is a single objective pursued for weeks under a compute budget fixed in advance, and a restarted run has spent its budget. Give a one-screen checklist of the decisions this module covers, each with its section: budget (s1), data and tokenizer (s2-s4), architecture (s5), optimiser and schedule (s6), precision and stabilisers (s7), memory and parallel layout (s8-s10), checkpointing and monitoring (s11), evaluation (s12), small runs, mid-training and continued pretraining (s13-s14).

The running case study, recalled from Module 07 and explicitly hypothetical: an engineering team adapts an open-weight bilingual English-Chinese model of about 9.5B parameters, released as base and instruct checkpoints, to draft and check safety-case arguments for the pressure-relief system of a reactor vessel. This module uses it twice. (a) How such a base is made: the 2T-token, 80-H100 plan worked through s1 and s4-s11 (budget, mixture, shape, schedule, memory, layout, failures), which the team will never run but needs in order to judge the base it adopts (its tokenizer, data, context length, the failures its makers had to manage). (b) The team's own decision, costed in s14: whether to continue pretraining the base on 2B tokens of safety-engineering text (1.8B domain plus 0.2B replay, 1,907 steps), gated by baselines and a go/no-go rule fixed in advance. Module 09 post-trains from the result (the continued-pretraining checkpoint if it is kept, otherwise the instruct release) and Module 10 serves the merged, quantised model. Configuration (Module 07's; counted in s5): L = 36, d = 4,096, 32 query and 8 KV heads of 128, SwiGLU d_ff = 15,360, V = 152,064, untied embeddings; N = 9,550,729,216, written 9.5B in prose (the source's tables round to 9.5B, 0.5% low). It is a worked case the reader follows, not anyone's plan or product.

The FLOP rule, recalled rather than derived (Module 06, Section 11 derives it and owns the convention; one paragraph and a link): a weight used in a matrix multiply costs 2 FLOPs per token in the forward pass and the backward pass costs twice the forward, hence the familiar $C \approx 6ND$. The series counts precisely: forward cost $2N_{\text{matmul}}$ per token, where $N_{\text{matmul}} = N - Vd$ leaves out the input embedding (a lookup), plus $4Ldt$ for a token at context position $t$, which averages to $2LdT$ over a causal sequence of length $T$; training costs three times the forward. Memory and Chinchilla's $N$ use all parameters. State the rule once here and say which count every later figure uses.

The rule applied to the case study (worked example): forward $1.79 \times 10^{10}$ FLOPs per token; training $5.36 \times 10^{10}$ plus $6LTd = 7.25 \times 10^9$ at $T = 8{,}192$ (+13.5%), $6.08 \times 10^{10}$ in all. The shortcut $6N$ over all 9.55B parameters ($5.73 \times 10^{10}$) is 7% high on the weight term (the embedding lookup is free) and, by leaving out attention, 6% low overall: usable only as a labelled estimate. Conventions also differ between papers (PaLM's MFU counts $12LTd$, attention without the causal halving), so an MFU figure must say which count it used.

From FLOPs to time: GPU-hours = C / (peak x MFU x 3,600). Peak is the vendor's dense bf16 tensor-core figure (H100 SXM: 989 TFLOP/s, the series' assumed peak as of 2026; the doubled 'with sparsity' figure never applies to dense training). MFU (model FLOPs utilisation) is achieved model FLOPs per second over peak; 35-45% is good at scale; 0.40 x 989 = 396 TFLOP/s, which the source rounds to 4 x 10^14 FLOP/s sustained per H100, the assumption Modules 07-09 share.
MFU versus HFU: hardware FLOPs utilisation also counts recomputed activations (s8), so it is higher for the same run; MFU is the figure to quote and compare.

The source's budget table, kept with its five rows (9.5B on 190B, 2T and 15T tokens; 1B on 20B; 9.5B continued pretraining on 2B) and recomputed with the source's own arithmetic (6N with N = 9.5B, attention left out), with the correction that 7,500 GPU-hours on 16 GPUs is about 20 days, not a month. Then the case study under the series' rule: the 2T-token plan is 1.22 x 10^23 FLOPs and 44.0 days on 80 GPUs at 4 x 10^14 FLOP/s (6N over all parameters with no attention gives 41.5 days, and the source's 9.5B rounding 41.2); the continued pretraining is 1.22 x 10^20 FLOPs, 84.5 GPU-hours (s14). From here on the text uses the series' figures for the case study and says so.

Compute-optimal versus over-trained, recalled from Module 07 (Sections 4-5 derive the allocation and the over-training break-even and own them; one paragraph and a link). The Chinchilla fit is written in this module with its numbers, $L(N, D) = 1.69 + 406.4/N^{0.34} + 410.7/D^{0.28}$ nats per token, so that B always means a batch. About 20 tokens per parameter gives the lowest loss per training FLOP by the paper's first two methods, while the fitted law's own minimum sits at 40-80 tokens per parameter for C = 10^20 to 10^23; over-training at 100-2,000 tokens per parameter pays when inference dominates, because the lifetime cost is $6ND_{\text{train}} + 2ND_{\text{served}}$. Its limits: the constants belong to one corpus and tokenizer, and it was fitted on 70M-16B parameters trained on 5B-500B tokens.

The compute decision for how such a base is made, with the fit used as Chinchilla accounted (6ND over all parameters): at the case study's budget the fitted minimum is 15.5B parameters on 1.23T tokens, the 20-tokens point 30.9B on 618B, and the case study 9.55B on 2T; all three predict losses within 0.007 nats, so the smallest is chosen for its 1.6 to 3.2 times cheaper serving. The compute-optimal model of equal predicted loss (15.0B on 1.18T tokens) would cost 7% less to train; the extra training is repaid after 7.4 x 10^11 served tokens, about 170 years of the team's own 12M tokens a day (Module 07's workload: 2,000 requests of 4,000 input and 2,000 output tokens) but 74 days at 10^10 tokens a day. Over-training pays back over every token a base serves for all its users: it is the base producer's decision, and one reason a team adopts an over-trained open base rather than training its own.

Why the plan is set at 2T tokens (about 210 tokens per parameter): 84,500 H100-hours, about USD 211,000 of GPU time at the series' assumed USD 2.50 per GPU-hour (an assumption, as of 2026; ablations, failed runs and staff not included), is a budget a well-funded organisation could commit; it sits in the over-trained regime that makes a small model worth serving; the 15T row shows what the strongest open models of this size are trained on (as of 2026, stated conservatively).
worked_examples: The source's table recomputed with the source's own arithmetic (6N with N = 9.5B, attention left out) at 4 x 10^14 FLOP/s per H100: 9.5B x 190B -> C = 6 x 9.5e9 x 1.9e11 = 1.08 x 10^22 FLOPs -> 7,521 GPU-hours -> 470 h = 19.6 days on 16 GPUs (correcting 'a month'); 9.5B x 2T -> 1.14 x 10^23 -> 79,167 h -> 41.2 days on 80 GPUs; 9.5B x 15T -> 8.55 x 10^23 -> 593,750 h -> 309 days, about 10 months, on 80 GPUs; 1B x 20B -> 1.2 x 10^20 -> 83 h -> 21 h on 4 GPUs (a weekend); 9.5B continued pretraining on 2B -> 1.14 x 10^20 -> 79 h -> 9.9 h on 8 GPUs.

The case study's FLOPs per token under the series' rule (L = 36, d = 4,096, T = 8,192): N_matmul = 9,550,729,216 - 622,854,144 = 8,927,875,072; forward 2N_matmul = 1.79 x 10^10; training 6N_matmul = 5.36 x 10^10; causal attention 6LTd = 6 x 36 x 8,192 x 4,096 = 7.25 x 10^9 (+13.5%; +6.8% at T = 4,096); total 6.08 x 10^10. The shortcut 6N over all parameters gives 5.73 x 10^10: 7% above the weight term, 6% below the total. At T = 131,072 the attention term is 1.16 x 10^11, 2.2 times the weight term, so a long-context token costs 2.8 times an 8k-context token (used again in s14).

The 2T-token plan under the series' rule: C = 6.08 x 10^10 x 2 x 10^12 = 1.22 x 10^23 FLOPs -> 84,465 GPU-hours at 4 x 10^14 FLOP/s -> 44.0 days on 80 GPUs; with 6N over all parameters and no attention, 1.15 x 10^23 FLOPs and 41.5 days. At the exact peak, 40% of 989 TFLOP/s gives 85,405 GPU-hours and 44.5 days; 30% MFU gives 59.3 days. MFU is a calendar quantity.

The compute decision at the case study's budget, with the fit as Chinchilla accounted (C = 6 x 9.55 x 10^9 x 2 x 10^12 = 1.146 x 10^23): fitted minimum N = 15.5B, D = 1.23T, L = 1.999; 20 tokens per parameter N = 30.9B, D = 618B, L = 2.005; the case study L = 1.69 + 0.164 + 0.148 = 2.002. The equal-loss compute-optimal model is 15.0B on 1.18T tokens, C' = 1.065 x 10^23 (7.6% less); break-even (1.146 - 1.065) x 10^23 / (2 x (15.0 - 9.55) x 10^9) = 7.4 x 10^11 served tokens: 62,000 days (170 years) at the case study's 1.2 x 10^7 tokens a day, 74 days at 10^10. Caveat in the text: 2T tokens lies outside the 5B-500B range the law was fitted on, so the comparison is indicative.

checks: What does the shortcut 6ND get wrong for the case study at T = 8,192? -> It counts the input embedding, a lookup that costs no FLOPs (7% high on the weight term), and leaves out causal attention, 6LTd per token (+13.5%); net it is 6% low.

A team reports 55% MFU with activation recomputation counted in the FLOPs. Is it comparable with another team's 45% MFU? -> No; counting recomputed FLOPs makes it HFU, inflated by up to a third (one extra forward pass); recompute it with model FLOPs only.

A 15B model on 1.18T tokens would match the case study's predicted loss for 7.6% less training compute. Why is the base trained at 9.55B on 2T? -> Every served token costs 2N FLOPs; the extra training is repaid after about 7.4 x 10^11 served tokens, which a widely used base serves quickly, although one team's 12M tokens a day never would.

sections.title: Data I: sources, extraction, language and quality filters
sections.purpose: Turn crawled and collected text into clean candidate documents, with each filter's rule, its threshold, and what it wrongly removes.
must_cover: Data quality is the largest lever after scale, and the pipeline is most of the engineering (source's framing).

Sources: Common Crawl (monthly snapshots of billions of web pages; WARC files hold the raw HTTP responses, WET files its own plain-text extraction), code repositories, books, academic papers, reference works, forums; for a bilingual model such as the case study, the Chinese web, books and academic text in proportion to the target use. Licensing and consent are unsettled and vary by jurisdiction; robots.txt opt-outs are honoured at crawl time; the corpus manifest records, per component, the source, snapshot or date, licence, filters applied and token count, and is the minimum record.

Text extraction: navigation, cookie banners, footers and repeated headers removed with extractors built for the purpose (trafilatura and its kind) run on the WARC HTML rather than taking the WET text; the FineWeb authors measured that this choice alone trained better models. Encoding repair belongs here too: UTF-8 text mis-decoded as Windows-1252 ('mojibake', e.g. 'â€”' for an em dash) survives every quality rule; Lab 1 finds it in about 6% of the TinyStories stories, and Lab 2's model learns to emit it.

Language identification: a linear classifier over character n-gram features (fastText's language-ID model is the common one) gives a score per language; keep documents whose top score exceeds a threshold (e.g. 0.65) at the proportions wanted. Failures: short texts, code-mixed text (English-Chinese technical writing), closely related languages and scripts.

Heuristic quality filters with the Gopher thresholds (Rae et al. 2021), each stated as a rule: 50-100,000 words; mean word length 3-10 characters; hash-or-ellipsis-to-word ratio at most 0.1; at most 90% of lines starting with a bullet; at most 30% of lines ending with an ellipsis; at least 80% of words containing an alphabetic character; at least two of the stop words {the, be, to, of, and, that, have, with}; repetition rules (duplicate-line fraction at most 0.30, duplicate-paragraph fraction at most 0.30, characters in the most frequent 2-, 3- and 4-gram at most 20%, 18%, 16%, characters in duplicated 5- to 10-grams at most 15% down to 10%).

C4's line-level rules (Raffel et al. 2020) as the contrast: keep only lines ending in terminal punctuation, drop pages containing 'lorem ipsum' or a curly bracket, drop pages with words from a blocklist; the curly-bracket rule removes almost all code, which is why code needs its own pipeline.
Rules are language-specific: word-based rules do not apply to Chinese, which has no spaces between words; use character-based equivalents and a Chinese stop-word list.

Model-based quality filters: a small classifier trained to separate reference-quality text from random web text scores every document; the corpus is thresholded or sampled by score. FineWeb-Edu: an LLM rated about 450,000 web pages for educational value on a 0-5 scale; a small classifier on top of an embedding model learned those ratings and scored all of FineWeb (about 15T tokens); keeping scores of 3 and above left about 1.3T tokens and improved knowledge and reasoning benchmarks for the same number of training tokens. DCLM's fastText classifier as the cheaper variant. The failure: the classifier encodes its annotator's taste (encyclopaedic, formal, English-centric) and narrows the corpus.

Personal data: regular expressions for e-mail addresses, phone numbers and IP addresses, replaced with placeholder tokens rather than deleted so the text stays fluent; names are hard and mostly left; over-matching damages technical text (version strings that look like IP addresses).

Toxicity and safety filtering: URL blocklists and classifiers. Dodge et al. (2021) found that C4's word blocklist disproportionately removed text written by and about minority groups. Removing all harmful text also removes the model's ability to recognise it, which post-training (Module 09) relies on.

Ordering by cost: cheap filters first (URL, language, heuristics), expensive ones (model classifiers, near-duplicate detection) on what survives; record why every document was removed, because that log is the debugging record when a later model is bad.
worked_examples: Three documents through the Gopher rules (writers use these texts verbatim, quoting (c) as inline code because the page would read its '$$$' as maths; Lab 1's function reproduces the numbers). (a) 'The bearing on the pump shaft ran hot for three days before the alarm. Wear on the outer race had loosened the fit, and the extra play let the shaft vibrate. The maintenance team replaced the bearing and checked the alignment with a dial gauge. They also changed the inspection interval from six months to three, because the vibration log showed the fault had been growing for weeks.' 68 words, mean word length 4.65, every word alphabetic, four stop words (and, the, to, with), no repeated lines: passes every rule. (b) The line 'Home | About us | Contact | Privacy policy | Login | Cart' repeated on 5 lines: 65 whitespace-separated words, so it passes the length rule, but only 61.5% of them contain a letter (the '|' tokens), it has no stop words, and 80% of its lines are duplicates: three failures. (c) 'BUY NOW!!! $$$ #deal CHEAP #sale watches FREE shipping >>>' repeated 8 times: 80 words, 16 hash tokens give a symbol ratio of 0.2 (> 0.1) and there are no stop words: two failures; it passes the alphabetic-word rule at exactly 80%.
FineWeb-Edu in proportion: 1.3T of 15T tokens kept at threshold 3, about 8.7% of the tokens.

checks: Why does the stop-word rule catch spam and navigation pages so cheaply? -> Natural prose almost always contains at least two of the eight commonest English function words; menus, lists and keyword spam rarely do.

A quality classifier trained to prefer Wikipedia-like text is applied to maintenance logs. sections.title: Data II: deduplication and decontamination
sections.purpose: Explain why duplicates hurt, derive MinHash and the LSH banding S-curve, and keep evaluation data out of the training set before it can inflate results.
must_cover: Why deduplicate: duplicates waste compute, raise memorisation and verbatim regurgitation, and tilt the mixture toward whatever was copied most. Lee et al. (2022): models trained on deduplicated C4 emit memorised text about ten times less often and reach the same or better accuracy in fewer steps. Hernandez et al. (2022): repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times degraded an 800M-parameter model to the performance of one half its size, although 90% of the training tokens stayed unique.

Exact deduplication: normalise (lower-case, collapse whitespace), hash (SHA-1 or a 64-bit hash), keep the first occurrence; the same at line and paragraph level across documents to strip repeated boilerplate; exact substring deduplication with suffix arrays (Lee et al. removed repeated spans of 50 tokens or more) as the fine-grained version.
Near-duplicates: shingle each document into word $n$-grams (5-grams here) and measure Jaccard similarity $J(A,B) = |A \cap B| / |A \cup B|$.

MinHash, derived: under a random permutation $\pi$ of the shingle universe, $P[\min \pi(A) = \min \pi(B)] = J(A,B)$, because the smallest element of $\pi(A \cup B)$ is equally likely to be any element of $A \cup B$, and the two minima coincide exactly when it lies in $A \cap B$. With $k$ independent hash functions, $\hat J = \frac{1}{k}\sum_i \mathbf{1}[h_i(A) = h_i(B)]$ is unbiased with variance $J(1-J)/k$. In practice a universal hash $h(x) = (ax + b) \bmod p$ stands in for a random permutation (Broder 1997).

LSH banding, derived: split the $k = br$ signature into $b$ bands of $r$ rows; a pair is a candidate if any band agrees in all $r$ rows. One band agrees with probability $s^r$; no band agrees with probability $(1 - s^r)^b$; so $P(\text{candidate}) = 1 - (1 - s^r)^b$, an S-curve whose steepest point is near $s^\ast \approx (1/b)^{1/r}$. More rows sharpen the curve and raise the threshold; more bands lower it.

Cost: comparing all pairs is n(n - 1)/2 comparisons; LSH hashes each document into b buckets and compares only within buckets; candidates are then verified (exact Jaccard, or signature agreement) and grouped into clusters with union-find, keeping one document per cluster.

Published choices: FineWeb used word 5-grams and 112 hashes in 14 bands of 8 (aimed at pairs about 75% similar) and found that deduplicating each crawl snapshot separately trained better models than deduplicating across all snapshots at once, because global deduplication left proportionally more of the older, lower-quality text.

How edits translate into Jaccard: replacing a fraction q of words leaves a fraction s = (1 - q)^n of n-gram shingles intact, so J is about s / (2 - s); longer shingles make near-copies look less similar.

Decontamination: remove training documents that share long n-grams with any evaluation set you will report (GPT-3 used 13-gram overlap); do it before training, keep the list of what was removed, and treat any public benchmark you did not decontaminate against as contaminated. False positives come from common phrases, licence text and famous quotations; false negatives from paraphrased or translated test items, which n-gram checks miss. Reading a contaminated claim is Module 07's topic; contamination of post-training sets is Module 09's.
worked_examples: MinHash standard error with k = 128: at J = 0.8, sqrt(0.8 x 0.2 / 128) = 0.035; at J = 0.5, 0.044; with k = 256 at J = 0.8, 0.025. Lab 1 measures a mean absolute error of about 0.03 against exact Jaccard.

The S-curve for b = 16, r = 8 (k = 128): threshold (1/16)^(1/8) = 0.71; P(candidate) = 0.001 at s = 0.3, 0.061 at 0.5, 0.237 at 0.6, 0.613 at 0.7, 0.815 at 0.75, 0.947 at 0.8, 0.994 at 0.85, 0.9999 at 0.9. FineWeb's b = 14, r = 8 (threshold 0.72): 0.053 at 0.5, 0.772 at 0.75, 0.924 at 0.8. A loose b = 32, r = 4 (threshold 0.42) makes 87% of pairs at s = 0.5 candidates, many more to verify; a strict b = 8, r = 16 (threshold 0.88) catches only 20% of pairs at s = 0.8.

Edit rate to Jaccard with 5-word shingles: q = 0.01 -> s = 0.951, J = 0.91; q = 0.03 -> 0.75; q = 0.05 -> 0.63; q = 0.08 -> 0.49; q = 0.12 -> 0.36; q = 0.20 -> 0.20. A copy with one word in twenty changed is only 63% similar; with 13-word shingles the same copy scores 0.35.
Pair counts: 10^9 documents give 5 x 10^17 pairs; with 16 bands LSH makes 1.6 x 10^10 bucket insertions. Lab 1's 6,400 documents give 20.5 million pairs and about 750 candidates.

checks: Why is the MinHash collision probability exactly the Jaccard similarity? -> The smallest hashed element of A union B is equally likely to be any of its elements, and the two minima agree exactly when that element is in A intersect B.

With b = 16 and r = 8, what fraction of pairs with true Jaccard 0.6 become candidates, and does it matter? -> About 24%; they cost verification time, not correctness, as long as candidates are verified against a threshold.

Why decontaminate before training rather than drop the overlapping test items afterwards? -> Dropping items afterwards shrinks and biases the test set; decontaminating first keeps the full test set clean and the record of what was removed.

sections.title: Data III: mixtures, multilingual balance, the tokenizer and packing
sections.purpose: Choose the proportions of each source and language, fix the tokenizer before anything else, and turn documents into dense training sequences.
must_cover: A mixture is a set of weights w_s summing to 1; source s contributes w_s D tokens and is seen w_s D / U_s times (U_s = its unique tokens). Repetition: Muennighoff et al. (2023) found that up to about 4 epochs of repeated data is almost as good as fresh data, with value falling quickly beyond; small high-quality sources are deliberately repeated 2-4 times.

What sources buy (source's points, kept): proportions are chosen, not inherited; code improves reasoning-like tasks even outside code; a few percent of reference text and textbooks lifts the whole model; too much of any one source narrows it.

Tuning the mixture: proxy runs at 100M-1B parameters with candidate mixtures, compared on per-domain held-out loss and a small benchmark battery; DoReMi (Xie et al. 2023) learns domain weights with a small proxy model by up-weighting the domains where it lags a reference model; the mixture (or a staged schedule of mixtures) is then fixed for the big run. The risk: proxy rankings do not always transfer to the large model.

Multilingual balance by temperature sampling: sample language $l$ with probability $p_l \propto q_l^{\alpha}$, where $q_l$ is its share of the available data; $\alpha = 1$ keeps natural proportions, $\alpha \to 0$ approaches uniform, $\alpha = 0.3$ is common (mT5 used it). The cost: low-resource languages are repeated more, and at fixed capacity languages compete for parameters.

The tokenizer as a pipeline decision (the BPE algorithm is Module 07's): trained on a sample of the final mixture before anything else, because everything downstream is counted in its tokens; vocabulary size trades embedding parameters (V d, doubled if untied) and output-softmax cost (2dV FLOPs per token forward) against sequence length; 32k suits English, 100k-150k a bilingual or multilingual corpus; per-language compression decides how much context and compute each language gets; digits split into single characters (arithmetic improves); byte fallback so nothing is out of vocabulary; the special tokens the chat template will need (Module 09) reserved now; V padded to a multiple of 64 or 128 for kernel efficiency.

Packing: documents joined with an end-of-document token and cut into length-T sequences, so no compute is spent on padding. Attention across a document boundary inside a sequence is either allowed (simple, slightly harmful) or masked with a block-diagonal causal mask (correct, slightly more complex; Llama 3 masked and found it mattered most for long sequences). Long documents are split across sequences; best-fit packing (Ding et al. 2024) reduces the number of documents cut.

Shards and the loader: tokenised data stored as flat uint16 or uint32 arrays in shards; the loader's position (shard, offset, random state) is part of every checkpoint (s11), or a restart repeats or skips data.
worked_examples: The case study's hypothetical 2T-token mixture (unique tokens after filtering -> weight -> tokens -> epochs): English web 1,500B -> 50% -> 1,000B -> 0.67; Chinese web 600B -> 20% -> 400B -> 0.67; code 400B -> 15% -> 300B -> 0.75; academic papers 80B -> 6% -> 120B -> 1.5; books 50B -> 4% -> 80B -> 1.6; reference works 20B -> 2% -> 40B -> 2.0; mathematics 30B -> 3% -> 60B -> 2.0. Labelled hypothetical; every repeated source stays under 4 epochs.

Temperature sampling for three languages with shares (0.80, 0.15, 0.05): alpha = 0.7 -> (0.688, 0.213, 0.099); alpha = 0.5 -> (0.594, 0.257, 0.149); alpha = 0.3 -> (0.490, 0.297, 0.213). At alpha = 0.3 the smallest language is sampled 4.3 times as often as its natural share.

Vocabulary cost at d = 4,096: V = 32,000 -> 131M embedding parameters (262M untied), fp32 logits for one 8,192-token sequence 1.05 GB, output head 0.26 GFLOP per token forward; V = 152,064 -> 623M (1.25B untied), 4.98 GB, 1.25 GFLOP.

Packing versus padding on Lab 2's data (TinyStories validation split, the lab's 4,096-token BPE): stories average 222 tokens including the end-of-text token (median 194, 90th percentile 333, longest 1,120). Padding every story to 512 tokens wastes 57% of the compute and still truncates 2.9% of stories; padding to 256 wastes 23% and truncates 19%; packing into 256-token windows wastes nothing.

figures.description: Packing: five documents of different lengths (coloured bars) laid end to end with EOD markers and cut into fixed-length rows of T tokens; beside it the T x T attention mask for one row that spans three documents: the full causal triangle (cross-document attention allowed) and the block-diagonal causal version with the cross-document blocks greyed out.

checks: A 20B-token source gets 2% of a 2T-token run. How many epochs is that, and is it a problem? -> 40B / 20B = 2 epochs, within the range where repetition costs little (up to about 4).

Why train the tokenizer on the final mixture rather than on English web text alone? -> A tokenizer trained on English compresses Chinese and code poorly, so those sources cost more tokens (compute and context) per character and get no merges for their frequent strings.

sections.title: Architecture at scale: sizes, mixture of experts, muP
sections.purpose: Size a decoder to a parameter budget, explain what changes when its FFNs become a mixture of experts at scale, and show how hyperparameters found on a small model are carried to a large one.
must_cover: The parameter count of the modern block (Module 06) in general form: per layer $d\,(n_h d_h) + 2d\,(n_{kv} d_h) + (n_h d_h)\,d + 3 d\, d_{ff} + 2d$, plus embeddings $Vd$ (twice if untied) and a final norm. With $n_h d_h = d$ and $n_{kv} = n_h/4$ this is $(2.5 + 3d_{ff}/d)\,d^2$ per layer: $13d^2$ at $d_{ff} = 3.5d$ (Llama 3 8B), $13.75d^2$ at the case study's $3.75d$; the source's $12Ld^2$ comes from multi-head attention with a $4d$ GELU MLP, or a SwiGLU at $d_{ff} = 8d/3$.
The 8/3 rule derived: a GELU MLP with hidden width 4d has 2 x d x 4d = 8d^2 parameters; SwiGLU has three matrices, so d_ff = 8d/3 keeps the count; many recent models use 3-3.75d with fewer layers.

The case study's configuration (Module 07's model, hypothetical; here also the shape the plan of s1 trains): L = 36, d = 4,096, 32 query heads of dimension 128, 8 KV heads (GQA groups of 4), SwiGLU d_ff = 15,360, RMSNorm pre-norm plus a final norm, RoPE base 500,000, context 8,192 in pretraining, vocabulary 152,064 (English-Chinese byte-level BPE), untied embeddings, no biases: 9,550,729,216 parameters, 8.31B in the blocks and 1.25B in the two embedding tables.

The source's decision table, kept with one line of reason per row: layers 32-42; width 3,584-4,096; heads / KV heads 28-32 / 4-8 (GQA groups of 4-8); head dimension 128 (convention and kernel efficiency); SwiGLU FFN; RMSNorm pre-norm with a final norm; RoPE base 10^4-10^6 (larger for longer intended context); vocabulary 128k-152k for bilingual, tied or untied; pretraining context 4k-8k, extended in mid-training (long context from the start is wasteful); no biases; dense at this size, MoE above roughly 30B active parameters as a rule of thumb.

Width versus depth: at fixed N the loss is nearly flat over a wide range of shapes (Kaplan et al. 2020 found a few percent across aspect ratios d/L from about 20 to 200; the case study's is 114); deeper is slower per token and adds pipeline stages; decide N first, then shape by precedent and kernel-friendly sizes (multiples of 128). Architectural switches are ablated at 100M-1B and assumed to transfer, which they mostly do; the exceptions are what the literature is about.

Mixture of experts at LLM scale (the concept is Module 05's): each FFN replaced by E expert FFNs and a router (a d x E linear layer and a softmax); each token goes to its top-k experts and their outputs are summed with the router weights. Compute per token follows the active parameters; memory follows the total.

Expert parallelism: experts spread across GPUs; tokens dispatched to their experts by an all-to-all and returned by a second all-to-all; per token per MoE layer that is about 2 x k x d x 2 bytes in bf16, usually across nodes, so it is the bottleneck to design around.

Load balancing: without it the router collapses onto a few experts. Switch-style auxiliary loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha E \sum_i f_i P_i$, with $f_i$ the fraction of tokens dispatched to expert $i$ and $P_i$ the mean router probability for expert $i$; it equals $\alpha$ at perfect balance; $f_i$ is not differentiable, so the gradient flows through $P_i$, weighted by $f_i$. Capacity factor CF: each expert processes at most $\text{CF}\cdot kT/E$ tokens per batch, and overflow tokens are dropped (they pass through the residual connection unchanged). Auxiliary-loss-free balancing (DeepSeek-V3): a per-expert bias added to the routing scores for top-k selection only, nudged down for overloaded experts and up for idle ones. Fine-grained and shared experts (DeepSeekMoE) at concept level.

When MoE pays: published MoEs (Mixtral 8x7B: 46.7B total, 12.9B active parameters per token; DeepSeek-V3: 671B total, 37B active) trade memory and communication for FLOPs; at the case study's 9.5B a dense model is the norm because MoE's memory and engineering costs outweigh the FLOP saving.

muP at concept level: under the standard parametrisation the best learning rate drifts as width grows, so a sweep at width 256 does not transfer to 4,096. With Adam each update entry has size about eta whatever the gradient's scale; a hidden matrix with fan-in n sums n such coherent contributions per output, so the output changes by about eta n; keeping that change of order one requires eta proportional to 1/n for hidden matrices. muP (Yang et al. 2021) applies this together with matching initialisation and output-logit scaling, so the best learning rate found on a narrow proxy holds for the wide model. Alternatives used in practice: power laws for the best learning rate and batch size fitted against compute (DeepSeek LLM, 2024), or plain sweeps at two or three scales.
worked_examples: The case-study count: attention per layer 4,096 x 4,096 (Q) + 2 x 4,096 x 1,024 (K, V) + 4,096 x 4,096 (O) = 41,943,040; SwiGLU 3 x 4,096 x 15,360 = 188,743,680; two norms 8,192; per layer 230,694,912 (13.75 d^2); x 36 = 8,305,016,832; embeddings 152,064 x 4,096 = 622,854,144 each, two untied tables 1,245,708,288; final norm 4,096; total 9,550,729,216, about 9.55B (Module 07 quotes the same count). 12Ld^2 = 7.25B would under-count the blocks by 1.06B: d_ff = 3.75d puts 11.25d^2 in each FFN where the rule assumes 8d^2, and GQA saves 1.5d^2 of attention's 4d^2.

The same arithmetic on another shape: L = 32, d = 4,096, 32/8 heads, d_ff = 14,336, V = 128,256, untied gives 6,979,584,000 + 1,050,673,152 + 4,096 = 8,030,261,248, the published 8.03B of Llama 3 8B (Lab 4 checks this).

The case study as an MoE: each FFN replaced by 8 experts of the same size with top-2 routing (a 4,096 x 8 router per layer): 57.1B total parameters, 16.3B active per token (15.7B of them in matrix multiplies); training FLOPs per token 6 x 15.7 x 10^9 + 7.25 x 10^9 (attention) = 1.02 x 10^11, 1.7 times the dense model's 6.08 x 10^10, but model states 16 x 57.1B = 914 GB (6.0 times). All-to-all traffic 2 x 2 x 4,096 x 2 bytes = 32 KB per token per MoE layer.

Load-balancing loss with E = 4: f = (0.55, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15), P = (0.50, 0.167, 0.167, 0.167) -> E x sum f_i P_i = 4 x (0.275 + 3 x 0.025) = 1.40, against 1.00 at perfect balance; the gradient lowers P_1 hardest because f_1 is largest.
Capacity: 8,192 tokens per device, k = 2, E = 8, CF = 1.25 -> 2,560 slots per expert; an expert attracting 30% of the 16,384 routed assignments (4,915) drops 2,355 of them.

muP transfer: best hidden-matrix learning rate 1 x 10^-2 at width 256 -> 1 x 10^-2 x 256 / 4,096 = 6.25 x 10^-4 at width 4,096 (hidden matrices only; embedding and output layers follow different rules).

checks: Why do total parameters set an MoE's memory but active parameters set its FLOPs? -> Every expert's weights and optimiser states must be stored, but each token passes through only k experts.

In the auxiliary loss f_i is not differentiable. How does the loss still balance load? -> The gradient flows through P_i, weighted by f_i, so router probability is pushed down hardest for the experts that receive the most tokens.

Why must a learning rate tuned at width 256 come down at width 4,096 under the standard parametrisation with Adam? -> Adam's update entries have a fixed size, and a wider matrix sums more of them into each output, so the same eta changes the outputs more; the change grows with fan-in.

sections.title: The optimiser recipe: AdamW, schedules, batch size
sections.purpose: Set the optimiser, the learning-rate schedule and the batch size for a long run, with the reason for every number.
must_cover: AdamW reminder (Module 02 owns it): $m \leftarrow \beta_1 m + (1-\beta_1) g$, $v \leftarrow \beta_2 v + (1-\beta_2) g^2$, bias correction, $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,(\hat m/(\sqrt{\hat v} + \epsilon) + \lambda\theta)$. Pretraining settings: $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.95$, $\epsilon = 10^{-8}$, $\lambda = 0.1$ on weight matrices only (not norms or biases, and in many recipes not embeddings).

Why beta2 = 0.95 rather than 0.999: the second-moment average remembers about 1/(1 - beta2) steps (20 versus 1,000); with a long memory a sudden rise in gradient scale meets a stale, small v and produces an oversized step.

epsilon: when gradient RMS falls toward epsilon (large or deep models late in training) the update is damped; Wortsman et al. (2024) lowered it (to about 10^-15) for this reason. Llama 2 used 10^-5; the source's 10^-8 is a common default.
Weight decay as a timescale: decoupled decay multiplies weights by (1 - eta lambda) each step, a forgetting time of 1/(eta lambda) steps, to be compared with the length of the run.

The learning rate is the most important number in the run: set from a sweep at small scale plus muP or a fitted scaling rule; larger models need smaller peaks. Anchor with a published recipe: Llama 2 used a peak of 3 x 10^-4 for its 7B and 13B models and 1.5 x 10^-4 for 34B and 70B, with 2,000 warmup steps, cosine decay to 10% of the peak, a 4M-token batch and clipping at 1.0. The source's 'about 1 x 10^-4 at 10B' is softened to '1-3 x 10^-4 at 7-10B, lower for larger models'.

Warmup, linear over the first 1,000-2,000 steps, with the reasons: Adam's v starts from too few samples; early gradients are large and the curvature high; the first steps at full rate can push the model into a region it never leaves (Lab 3 shows a version of this).

Warmup-cosine, written out: $\eta(t) = \eta_{\max}\, t / T_w$ for $t < T_w$, then $\eta_{\min} + \tfrac{1}{2}(\eta_{\max} - \eta_{\min})\big(1 + \cos(\pi (t - T_w)/(T - T_w))\big)$ with $\eta_{\min} = 0.1\,\eta_{\max}$. Its weakness: the horizon $T$ must be fixed before the run starts.

Warmup-stable-decay (WSD): warmup, a long constant phase at the peak, then a short decay (about 10-20% of steps) to near zero; it matches cosine at the same budget (Hägele et al. 2024; MiniCPM popularised it) and lets the run be extended, or a decay branched from any stable-phase checkpoint, so one run yields models for several budgets. The loss falls sharply during the decay: noise is being averaged out, not new knowledge learned.

Batch size, measured in tokens: 1M-4M tokens per step at 9B scale, sometimes ramped up during the run. The critical batch size (McCandlish et al. 2018), derived from a quadratic model of the loss: with mean gradient $G$, Hessian $H$ and per-example gradient covariance $\Sigma$, a plain SGD step with learning rate $\eta$ on a batch of $B$ changes the loss by $-\eta|G|^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\eta^2(G^\top H G + \mathrm{tr}(H\Sigma)/B)$ (McCandlish et al. write $\epsilon$; $\eta$ avoids a clash with Adam's epsilon); the best step gives $\Delta L_{\text{opt}}(B) = \Delta L_{\max}/(1 + B_{\text{noise}}/B)$ with $B_{\text{noise}} = \mathrm{tr}(H\Sigma)/G^\top H G$ (simplified, $\mathrm{tr}\,\Sigma/|G|^2$). Hence steps $S = S_{\min}(1 + B_{\text{noise}}/B)$ and tokens processed $D = SB = D_{\min}(1 + B/B_{\text{noise}})$ (McCandlish et al. write $E$ for examples; here $D$ keeps the module's symbol for tokens, because $E$ is already the number of experts in s5), so $(S/S_{\min} - 1)(D/D_{\min} - 1) = 1$; at $B = B_{\text{crit}} = B_{\text{noise}}$ both are twice their minimum. $B_{\text{noise}}$ grows as the loss falls, which justifies batch-size ramps.
Gradient accumulation decouples the effective batch from memory: global batch = micro-batch x accumulation steps x data-parallel degree.
Learning rate and batch move together: below the critical batch a larger batch tolerates a larger learning rate (roughly linearly for SGD, closer to square-root for Adam); confirm with a sweep.
worked_examples: beta2 and an outlier gradient: steady gradient RMS 10^-3 (v = 10^-6), then one gradient of 10^-2 with m starting near zero, so m = 10^-3. With beta2 = 0.999, v = 1.099 x 10^-6 and the step is m / sqrt(v) = 0.954 eta; with beta2 = 0.95, v = 5.95 x 10^-6 and the step is 0.410 eta. If the gradient stays ten times larger, v reaches half its new level in 14 steps at 0.95 and 683 steps at 0.999.

Weight-decay timescale: eta = 3 x 10^-4 and lambda = 0.1 give 1/(eta lambda) = 33,333 steps; the case-study plan has 508,626 steps, so weights forget their early values about 15 times over; Lab 2's eta = 3 x 10^-3 gives 3,333 steps, longer than its 600-step run.

The case-study schedule: global batch 480 sequences x 8,192 = 3,932,160 tokens (close to Llama 2's 4M); 2T / 3.93M = 508,626 steps; warmup 2,000 steps (0.4%); peak 3 x 10^-4; cosine to 3 x 10^-5: eta = 1.5 x 10^-4 at step 1,000, 3.0 x 10^-4 at 2,000, 2.61 x 10^-4 at 127,000, 1.66 x 10^-4 at the midpoint 254,313, 7.0 x 10^-5 at 381,000 and 3.0 x 10^-5 at the end.

Critical batch with B_noise = 2M tokens: B = 0.25M -> S/S_min = 9.0, D/D_min = 1.12; 0.5M -> 5.0, 1.25; 1M -> 3.0, 1.5; 2M -> 2.0, 2.0; 4M -> 1.5, 3.0; 8M -> 1.25, 5.0; 16M -> 1.12, 9.0. Below B_noise, doubling the batch nearly halves the steps for little extra data; above it, the data bill climbs.

figures.description: Learning rate against step for a 10,000-step example with 500 warmup steps: warmup-cosine to 10% of the peak, WSD with the last 20% decaying linearly to zero, and a constant rate. Below it, schematic loss curves (labelled schematic): WSD's loss sits above cosine's through the stable phase and drops below it during the decay.

Steps versus tokens to reach a fixed loss: the hyperbola (S/S_min - 1)(D/D_min - 1) = 1 on log-log axes, points labelled with B = 0.25M ... 16M for B_noise = 2M, the critical batch at (2, 2) marked, and the two regimes labelled 'data-efficient' and 'time-efficient'.

checks: With beta2 = 0.95, roughly how many steps does Adam's second-moment estimate remember? -> About 1/(1 - beta2) = 20 steps.

What does a WSD schedule let you do that a cosine schedule does not? -> Extend or stop the run at any point; a decay can be branched from any stable-phase checkpoint, so one run gives models for several budgets.
At B = B_crit, how many steps and tokens does the run need compared with their minima? -> Twice each.

sections.title: Stability and precision: clipping, z-loss, QK-norm, bf16 and fp8
sections.purpose: Explain the number formats a run uses and the small additions that keep a long run from diverging.
must_cover: The formats, as a table: fp32 (1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 mantissa bits; max 3.4 x 10^38; relative spacing 2^-23, about 1.2 x 10^-7); fp16 (1/5/10; max 65,504; smallest normal 6.1 x 10^-5; smallest subnormal 6.0 x 10^-8; spacing 2^-10, about 9.8 x 10^-4); bf16 (1/8/7; fp32's range; spacing 2^-7, about 7.8 x 10^-3); fp8 E4M3 (max 448; spacing 2^-3) and E5M2 (max 57,344; spacing 2^-2).

Mixed precision as run (source's recipe, expanded): matmul inputs in bf16 with fp32 accumulation; fp32 master weights and optimiser states; softmax, norms and the loss computed in fp32. Master weights exist because a small update added to a bf16 weight rounds away.

fp16 needs loss scaling (Micikevicius et al. 2018): multiply the loss by S so small gradients become representable, unscale before the update; dynamic scaling halves S and skips the step on an inf or NaN, and doubles S after a run of clean steps (e.g. 2,000). fp16 is also prone to overflow in attention. bf16 has fp32's exponent range and needs no scaling: the reason modern runs are stable.

fp8: E4M3 for weights and activations in the forward pass, E5M2 (more range) for gradients in some recipes; per-tensor scale factors from a history of maximum absolute values, or fine-grained block scaling (DeepSeek-V3: 1 x 128 tiles for activations, 128 x 128 blocks for weights) with higher-precision accumulation; used for the large matmuls only, with care, in the newest runs (as of 2026).

Gradient clipping by global norm: $g \leftarrow g \cdot \min(1, c/\lVert g\rVert_2)$ over all parameters together, $c = 1.0$. Log the fraction of clipped steps: a run that clips most steps is running at a lower effective learning rate and hiding a problem.

z-loss: $\mathcal{L}_z = 10^{-4}(\log Z)^2$ with $Z = \sum_j e^{z_j}$; derive $\partial\mathcal{L}_z/\partial z_j = 2\cdot10^{-4}\,\log Z\,\mathrm{softmax}(z)_j$. Why it is needed: cross-entropy is unchanged if a constant is added to every logit, so nothing else pins their level, and logits that drift to large magnitudes lose precision in bf16 and can overflow; z-loss pulls $\log Z$ toward 0.

Attention-logit growth and QK-norm: $q\cdot k/\sqrt{d_h}$ can grow without bound as the query and key projections grow; the softmax saturates to one-hot, attention entropy collapses and training stalls or diverges (Dehghani et al. 2023; Wortsman et al. 2024). Normalising $q$ and $k$ per head (RMSNorm with a learned gain) bounds the logits: with unit-RMS $q$ and $k$ the logit is at most $d_h/\sqrt{d_h} = \sqrt{d_h} \approx 11.3$ (times the gains) for $d_h = 128$.
Other stabilisers at concept level: a lower peak learning rate, a longer warmup, no biases, a norm before the output head, scaled initialisation of residual projections.

Wortsman et al.'s method: small models at high learning rates reproduce the instabilities of large models, so mitigations can be tested cheaply by plotting final loss against learning rate ('learning-rate sensitivity'). Lab 3 does this on a laptop and finds, as they did, that the instability of a small model at a high rate is attention-logit growth, which QK-norm removes and which warmup, clipping and z-loss alone do not.
worked_examples: Why fp32 master weights: a weight of 0.02 lies in [2^-6, 2^-5), where bf16 spacing is 2^-13 = 1.22 x 10^-4; an update of 3 x 10^-5 (a late-run learning rate of 3 x 10^-5 times an Adam step of about 1) is below half a spacing (6.1 x 10^-5) and rounds to nothing, so the weight never moves (PyTorch confirms: bf16(0.02) + 3e-5 = bf16(0.02)). In fp32 the spacing at 0.02 is 1.9 x 10^-9.
Loss scaling in fp16: a gradient of 2 x 10^-8 is below fp16's smallest subnormal (5.96 x 10^-8) and becomes 0; multiplied by S = 65,536 it becomes 1.31 x 10^-3, comfortably representable.

bf16 precision of a drifted logit: at 30 (in [16, 32)) the bf16 spacing is 16 x 2^-7 = 0.125, so logits near 30 move in steps that change a probability ratio by e^0.125 = 1.13; near 4-8 the spacing is 0.031. With log Z = 30 and coefficient 10^-4, z-loss adds 2 x 10^-4 x 30 = 6 x 10^-3 x p_j to each logit's gradient, a steady pull back toward log Z = 0.
Clipping: a global norm of 4.0 with c = 1.0 multiplies every gradient entry by 0.25.

Lab 3's prototype numbers (writers replace them with the executed run): after 150 steps a 4-layer model at learning rate 3 x 10^-2 reached max |q.k|/sqrt(d_h) = 897 against 34 at 3 x 10^-3, and a loss of 5.44 against 4.58; adding warmup, clipping and z-loss left the logits between 600 and 1,300 and the loss at 5.37-5.46; adding QK-norm held the logits at 12 and the loss at 4.79. With all four stabilisers the loss at 3 x 10^-3 also improved, to 4.18.

checks: Why does bf16 not need loss scaling while fp16 does? -> bf16 has 8 exponent bits, fp32's range, so small gradients do not underflow; fp16 has 5 and flushes values below about 6 x 10^-8 to zero.
What does z-loss constrain that cross-entropy does not? -> The overall level of the logits (log Z); cross-entropy depends only on differences between logits.

A run clips 95% of its steps. What does that tell you? -> The effective learning rate is being set by the clip threshold rather than the schedule, and something (learning rate, data, a layer) is persistently producing large gradients.

sections.title: Memory accounting
sections.purpose: Count every byte a training step needs on a GPU, so that whether a configuration fits is a calculation rather than a trial.
must_cover: The 16-bytes-per-parameter rule, derived two ways: (a) bf16 weights 2 + bf16 gradients 2 + fp32 master weights 4 + Adam first moment 4 + Adam second moment 4 = 16; (b) PyTorch autocast with fp32 parameters: fp32 weights 4 + fp32 gradients 4 + m 4 + v 4 = 16, with bf16 copies of the weights made on the fly. Variants: fp32 gradient-accumulation buffers add 2 (18 bytes); 8-bit optimiser states give 2 + 2 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 10; plain SGD with momentum needs 4 bytes of state. ZeRO's paper writes this as 2 + 2 + K with K = 12.

Activations: what the backward pass needs from each layer (Module 02), counted for the case study's block with FlashAttention and no dropout, in bf16: the two norm inputs 2 x 2d, the QKV input 2d, Q 2d, K and V 2 x 2h_kv, the attention output 2d, the MLP input 2d, and the SwiGLU gate, up and their product 3 x 2d_ff, total 12d + 4h_kv + 6d_ff bytes per token per layer = 145,408 bytes = 35.5d for the case study. Say that implementations differ by perhaps 20% depending on what they fuse or recompute, and compare Korthikanti et al.'s 34 sbh for the original GPT block (dropout masks and GELU: different terms, a similar total).
Without FlashAttention the softmax probabilities add 2 n_h T^2 bytes per layer (more with dropout masks): the T^2 term FlashAttention removes by recomputing them blockwise in the backward pass.
The logits: T x V x 4 bytes in fp32 for the loss, often the largest single tensor in the step; chunked or fused cross-entropy computes the loss without materialising them all.

Activation checkpointing (also called gradient checkpointing): store each layer's input (2d bytes per token per layer) and recompute the layer's forward pass during the backward pass; memory falls to the stored inputs plus one layer's activations at a time; compute rises by one extra forward pass, from three forward-pass costs per token to four, about a third more. Selective checkpointing recomputes only the cheap, memory-heavy parts (attention scores, activation functions); segment checkpointing every sqrt(L) layers (Chen et al. 2016) gives O(sqrt(L)) memory for one extra forward pass.
Other consumers: communication buffers, temporary workspaces and allocator fragmentation (leave 5-10% headroom); CPU offload of optimiser states (ZeRO-Offload) as a slow escape hatch.
Contrast with inference: bf16 weights alone, 2 bytes per parameter, plus the KV cache (Module 10).
Units, stated once: GB = 10^9 bytes and GiB = 2^30 bytes; the module uses GB and gives GiB beside a figure that recurs in other modules (the case study's model states, 152.8 GB = 142.3 GiB).
worked_examples: Model states of the case study: 16 x 9.551 x 10^9 = 152.8 GB (142.3 GiB), the source's 152 GB; no single 80 GB GPU holds it, before a single activation.

Activations for one 8,192-token sequence: 145,408 x 8,192 x 36 = 42.9 GB (1.19 GB per layer); fp32 logits 8,192 x 152,064 x 4 = 4.98 GB. Without FlashAttention the bf16 attention probabilities alone are 2 x 32 x 8,192^2 = 4.29 GB per layer, 155 GB for 36 layers.

Full checkpointing: stored layer inputs 2 x 4,096 x 8,192 x 36 = 2.42 GB, plus one layer recomputed at a time 1.19 GB, gives 3.61 GB instead of 42.9 GB, for a third more compute (one extra forward pass per token).

Lab 2's model for scale: 5.8M parameters x 16 bytes = 93 MB of model states; activations for 16 x 256 tokens are of the same order; a laptop holds it easily, which is why the lab can skip every technique in this section.

sections.title: Data parallelism, ZeRO and FSDP
sections.purpose: Spread one model's training over many GPUs by replicating or sharding its states, with the memory and the communication of each option derived.
must_cover: Data parallelism: every GPU holds the whole model and a slice of the global batch; gradients are averaged by an all-reduce before the update, so the weights stay identical everywhere; its limit is that every GPU needs the whole model.

Ring all-reduce, derived: a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather around a ring of N_d GPUs, each in N_d - 1 steps of S/N_d bytes; each GPU sends and receives 2(N_d - 1)/N_d x S bytes, nearly independent of N_d; time about 2S/B_link for large N_d. Gradients are bucketed and reduced while the backward pass is still running, hiding most of the time.

ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al. 2020) with N parameters (Psi in the paper) on N_d GPUs and 12 bytes of optimiser state per parameter: plain DP 16N; stage 1 shards optimiser states, 4N + 12N/N_d; stage 2 also shards gradients, 2N + 14N/N_d; stage 3 also shards weights, 16N/N_d. Communication: stages 1 and 2 cost what DP costs (a reduce-scatter and an all-gather, 2N elements per step); stage 3 adds an all-gather of the weights in the backward pass, 3N, 1.5 times DP.

FSDP: PyTorch's implementation of stage 3, gathering each wrapped unit's weights just before use and freeing them after; prefetching overlaps the gather with compute. The trap: with gradient accumulation each micro-batch re-gathers the weights unless unsharded gradients are kept, which costs memory.
Hybrid sharding (HSDP): shard within a node over fast links, replicate across nodes, and all-reduce only each shard's gradients across nodes once per optimiser step.

Bandwidths to reason with (typical as of 2026; state them as such): NVLink inside an 8-GPU H100 node about 450 GB/s per direction per GPU (900 GB/s bidirectional); InfiniBand or RoCE between nodes about 50 GB/s per GPU (400 Gb/s per GPU).
The global-batch identity: global batch = micro-batch x accumulation steps x data-parallel degree; the parallel layout and the batch size are chosen together.
worked_examples: ZeRO on 8 GPUs for the case study (N = 9.551 x 10^9): DP 152.8 GB; ZeRO-1 4N + 12N/8 = 38.2 + 14.3 = 52.5 GB; ZeRO-2 2N + 14N/8 = 19.1 + 16.7 = 35.8 GB; ZeRO-3 16N/8 = 19.1 GB. On 80 GPUs ZeRO-3 needs 1.9 GB.

One 8 x 80 GB node with ZeRO-3: 19.1 (states) + 42.9 (activations, 1 x 8k) + 5.0 (logits) = 67.0 GB, which fits with 13 GB to spare; with full checkpointing 19.1 + 3.6 + 5.0 = 27.7 GB. With full checkpointing ZeRO-1 (61.1 GB) and ZeRO-2 (44.4 GB) also fit; without it, only ZeRO-3 does (ZeRO-2 needs 83.7 GB).

The gradient all-reduce for plain DP: bf16 gradients S = 19.1 GB; inside a node (N_d = 8 at 450 GB/s) each GPU sends 2 x 7/8 x 19.1 = 33.4 GB in 0.074 s; across 80 GPUs at 50 GB/s each sends 37.7 GB in 0.75 s.

sections.title: Tensor, pipeline and context parallelism; choosing a layout
sections.purpose: Split single layers, stacks of layers and long sequences across GPUs, derive what each costs, and combine them into a layout for a given model and cluster.
must_cover: Tensor parallelism (Megatron-LM, Shoeybi et al. 2019), derived for the MLP: $Y = \phi(XA)$ with $A$ split by columns $[A_1, A_2]$ gives $Y_i = \phi(XA_i)$ on GPU $i$ with no communication, because $\phi$ is elementwise; $Z = YB$ with $B$ split by rows gives $Z = Y_1B_1 + Y_2B_2$, summed by one all-reduce. For SwiGLU, gate and up are both column-split. Attention: heads split across GPUs (Q, K, V column-parallel by head), output projection row-parallel, one all-reduce. The conjugate operators f (identity forward, all-reduce backward) and g (all-reduce forward, identity backward) give two all-reduces per layer in the forward pass and two in the backward, each of b x T x d activations. With GQA the KV heads must divide by the TP degree or be replicated. Communication on every layer keeps TP inside a node (2-8 GPUs).

Sequence parallelism (Korthikanti et al. 2023): inside the TP group, the norm and dropout regions are split along the sequence; each all-reduce becomes a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather (same volume), and those activations are no longer replicated on every TP rank.

Pipeline parallelism: layers split into p stages; micro-batches keep the stages busy (GPipe; 1F1B). Bubble derivation: with m micro-batches, the schedule occupies (m + p - 1) slots of (t_f + t_b) and each stage is busy for m of them, so the idle fraction is (p - 1)/(m + p - 1) and the bubble relative to ideal compute is (p - 1)/m. 1F1B has the same bubble but holds activations for at most p micro-batches instead of m; interleaved stages (v virtual stages per GPU, Narayanan et al. 2021) cut the bubble to (p - 1)/(v m) for more communication. Activations cross stage boundaries point to point, a small volume, so pipelines suit slower inter-node links. Stages should hold equal numbers of layers: the case study's 36 layers split evenly over 2, 3, 4, 6 or 9 stages (and 12 or 18), one reason a layer count is chosen with the pipeline degrees it must support in mind.

Context parallelism for long sequences: the sequence split into chunks across GPUs; each GPU keeps its queries and passes key/value blocks around a ring (ring attention, Liu et al. 2024), overlapping the transfer with blockwise attention; causal masking makes contiguous chunks unequal in work, so chunks are interleaved to balance load; DeepSpeed-Ulysses as the alternative that uses all-to-all over heads.

A summary table of communication per GPU at case-study scale: DP all-reduce, 2N elements per optimiser step; ZeRO-3, 3N per micro-batch if weights are re-gathered; TP, 4 all-reduces of b T d per layer per micro-batch; PP, b T d point to point per micro-batch per stage boundary; CP, the K and V blocks of each layer; EP, two all-to-alls per MoE layer.

Choosing a layout, as a procedure: (1) does the model, with ZeRO over the node and a micro-batch of one sequence, fit with its activations? (2) if FSDP across nodes is communication-bound, shard within nodes and replicate across them (HSDP) or add TP inside the node; (3) if a layer's activations still do not fit, or the model is beyond roughly 30-70B, add PP across nodes; (4) for sequences of 32k tokens or more add CP; (5) set micro-batch and accumulation to hit the global batch; (6) measure MFU and iterate. Layouts are written DP x TP x PP (x CP) = number of GPUs. Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed, PyTorch FSDP and the stacks built on them implement all of it from a configuration.
The source's rule of thumb, kept: a 9.5B run on 64 GPUs might use TP 2 inside nodes and FSDP over the rest with no pipeline; a 70B run adds pipeline stages across nodes.
worked_examples: Pipeline bubbles: p = 4, m = 8 -> idle fraction 3/11 = 27% (37.5% of ideal); p = 4, m = 32 -> 8.6%; p = 8, m = 32 -> 17.9%; p = 8, m = 64 -> 9.9%; interleaved with v = 2 at p = 4, m = 8 -> bubble 18.8% of ideal.

TP traffic for the case study at TP = 2: each all-reduce carries b T d x 2 bytes = 1 x 8,192 x 4,096 x 2 = 67 MB; 4 per layer x 36 layers = 9.66 GB per GPU per micro-batch; at 450 GB/s that is 21 ms against about 0.62 s of compute per micro-batch at TP = 2 (3.4%; the series' FLOP rule at 4 x 10^14 FLOP/s); across nodes at 50 GB/s it would be 0.19 s (31%).

The case-study layout on 80 H100s (10 nodes of 8) for the 2T-token plan, global batch 480 x 8,192 = 3.93M tokens, so 6 micro-batches of 1 x 8k per GPU per step, each 1.25 s of compute under the series' rule at 4 x 10^14 FLOP/s: (a) plain DP: 152.8 GB per GPU, impossible; (b) ZeRO-1 over 80: 39.6 GB of states + 47.9 GB of activations and logits = 87.5 GB, does not fit without checkpointing; (c) FSDP over all 80: 1.9 GB of states, but each micro-batch moves 3 x 18.9 GB = 56.6 GB per GPU over 50 GB/s links, 1.13 s against 1.25 s of compute, which only near-perfect overlap would hide: communication-bound in practice; (d) HSDP: shard over the 8 GPUs of a node (19.1 GB of states; 3 x 16.7 = 50.1 GB per micro-batch over NVLink, 0.11 s) and replicate across the 10 nodes (one all-reduce of the 2.39 GB gradient shard per step, 4.3 GB sent, 0.086 s), with selective or full checkpointing for headroom: chosen. Compute per optimiser step 6 x 1.25 = 7.5 s; 508,626 steps take 44.0 days, matching s1.
Context parallelism: 131,072-token sequences with CP = 8 give 16,384 tokens per GPU and an eightfold cut in activation memory per GPU.

Why does FSDP over 80 GPUs struggle where HSDP does not? -> FSDP gathers weights over the slow inter-node links for every micro-batch; HSDP keeps the gathers on NVLink and crosses nodes once per step with a gradient shard.

sections.title: What breaks, and how a long run is operated
sections.purpose: Recognise how a long run fails (numerically, in its data, in its hardware) and set up the checkpoints and monitoring that make each failure recoverable.
must_cover: Loss spikes: the loss jumps and either recovers or diverges. Causes: a bad batch (garbage or an extreme document), a learning rate too high for a late-run sharpness, attention-logit growth, output-logit drift, fp16 overflow, a sudden gradient change meeting a stale Adam second moment. Remedies: bf16, z-loss, QK-norm, a lower peak rate, a longer warmup, and the operational one: rewind to a checkpoint before the spike and skip the offending batches (PaLM restarted from about 100 steps before a spike and skipped roughly 200-500 batches).
Divergence: the loss climbs steadily or becomes NaN; distinguished from a recoverable spike by the grad-norm trace; when the same data region always triggers it, suspect the data.

NaN and inf: sources (log of zero, division by a zero norm, fp16 overflow, a corrupted input); check loss and grad norm every step and skip the update when either is not finite; localise with anomaly detection on a small reproduction.

Data bugs that look like optimisation problems (source's examples, expanded with signatures): a shard duplicated many times (the training loss falls suspiciously while held-out loss stalls); the tokenizer of the data pipeline differs from the model's (loss stuck high from the start); padding or end-of-document tokens counted in the loss (the model learns to predict padding); shuffling broken (periodic structure in the loss); the loader restarted without its state (data repeated or skipped).

Hardware: GPU failures, nodes dropping out, network and filesystem stalls. Llama 3's report: 419 unexpected interruptions in a 54-day period of pretraining on up to 16,384 H100s, about one every 3 hours, roughly 78% attributed to confirmed or suspected hardware problems, with effective training time kept above 90% by automation. The run is a process, not an event.

Silent data corruption: a device that computes wrong numbers without raising an error (Dixit et al. 2021); detected by periodic known-answer tests, by comparing checksums of the replicated weights across data-parallel replicas, and by flagging per-replica loss or grad-norm outliers.

Checkpoints: their contents (weights, fp32 master weights, both optimiser moments, step, scheduler state, random-number-generator states, data-loader position, configuration, tokenizer hash); their size, about 12-14 bytes per parameter; asynchronous checkpointing (snapshot to host memory, write in the background); keep several and test restoring regularly.

The checkpoint interval, derived (Young 1974): with write time $\delta$ and mean time between failures $M$, the overhead per unit time is about $\delta/\tau + \tau/(2M)$ (writing, plus on average half an interval of lost work per failure); minimising gives $\tau^\ast = \sqrt{2\delta M}$.

Monitoring, each signal with what it catches: training loss per source; held-out loss; global and per-layer grad norm; per-layer update-to-weight ratio ||delta W|| / ||W|| (computed after each step; values around 10^-3 are typical with Adam at usual rates, and a layer far off that is mis-scaled); learning rate; fraction of clipped steps; maximum attention logit; mean output log Z; activation RMS per layer; loss scale (fp16 only); tokens per second and MFU; memory; data statistics (tokens per source, document length, end-of-document frequency). Every alert has a runbook entry.

Silent quality problems (source's last item): the loss looks fine and the model is bad because the mixture was wrong, evaluation data leaked, or the tokenizer split something important; s12's evaluation is the only detector.
worked_examples: Failure rates scaled to the case study: one interruption per 3.09 hours on 16,384 GPUs is about 50,700 GPU-hours per interruption; on 80 GPUs that is one per 633 hours, so the 44-day plan expects about 1.7 interruptions, if failures scale with GPU count.

Young's interval: delta = 60 s and M = 3.09 h (16k GPUs) give tau* = sqrt(2 x 60 x 11,124 s) = 19 minutes and an overhead of about 10%; delta = 60 s and M = 633 h (80 GPUs) give tau* = 4.6 hours and 0.7%. The source's warning made numerical: checkpoints every 5,000 steps of the case-study plan (5,000 x 7.5 s = 10.4 hours) lose about 5.2 hours of 80 GPUs on average per failure.

Checkpoint size: 12 bytes per parameter (fp32 master weights and both moments) = 115 GB for the case study, 134 GB with the bf16 weights; at 2 GB/s aggregate write that is 57-67 s, the delta used above.

sections.title: Evaluation during the run, and the base-model checkpoint
sections.purpose: Decide what to measure while the run is going so that a bad run is caught early, and describe what the finished base model is and is not.
must_cover: Held-out perplexity per source, every few hundred steps, on data removed from the mixture before training; and a held-out set of a different distribution (reference text the mixture did not include) to separate generalisation from memorisation.

Downstream tasks for a base model, scored by log-likelihood: for each multiple-choice item compute the sum of log p(option tokens | context) for each option, optionally normalised by the number of tokens or characters, and pick the highest; few-shot by prepending k solved examples; generation tasks (arithmetic, code checked by tests) need sampling and are noisier. Run a small battery (knowledge, arithmetic, code, reading, in each language of the mixture) every few thousand steps and plot it against tokens.

Noise: an accuracy on n items has standard error sqrt(p(1 - p)/n); small benchmarks cannot resolve small differences; downstream curves are noisier and less monotone than the loss, and some tasks sit at chance until the loss passes a level (Module 07's discussion of emergence).

The scaling-law check: predict the final loss from small runs, or fit L(D) = L_inf + a D^-gamma to the run's own early curve (not Chinchilla's letters, so B stays the batch), and compare as the run proceeds; a curve that departs from the prediction is the earliest sign of a data or recipe problem.

Choosing and averaging checkpoints: evaluate several late checkpoints; averaging the last few (or keeping an exponential moving average of the weights) gives a small free gain (pointer to Module 09's merging).

The base-model checkpoint (source s9, kept): weights, tokenizer, configuration, training log, data manifest with the decontamination record, evaluation curves. It completes text: asked a question it may answer or continue with more questions; asked for JSON it may produce JSON or an essay about JSON. Its knowledge is the corpus's up to the crawl date. It has no notion of a user, an instruction, a refusal or a tool; Module 09 gives it those. For the case study this is what the team receives with the open base it adopts; the data manifest and the decontamination record are often not released, one reason the team measures the base itself before deciding on continued pretraining (s14).
worked_examples: Standard errors: n = 500 items at 40% accuracy -> SE = sqrt(0.4 x 0.6 / 500) = 2.2 points, a 95% interval of +/- 4.3; n = 1,000 at 50% -> +/- 3.1; n = 14,042 (the size of MMLU's test set) at 60% -> +/- 0.8; Lab 2's 24-item cloze set at 50% -> +/- 20 points, which is why the lab's cloze accuracy jumps around.

Log-likelihood scoring and its normalisation trap: context 'The pump stopped, so the pressure' with options ' fell' (one token, log p = -1.2) and ' rose' (two tokens, -1.5 and -0.8, sum -2.3). By total log-probability ' fell' wins; per token (-1.2 against -1.15) ' rose' wins. The normalisation must be reported with the score.

sections.title: A small run you can actually do
sections.purpose: Turn the source's 125M-parameter recipe into a costed plan for one GPU, and connect it to the laptop-scale run of Lab 2.
must_cover: The source's recipe, kept as a block: data, a public cleaned web corpus (a FineWeb-Edu sample), 2-3B tokens, with a 32k BPE trained on it; model, 12 layers, d = 768, 12 heads, SwiGLU 2,048, RoPE, RMSNorm, tied embeddings; schedule, AdamW (0.9, 0.95), weight decay 0.1, peak 6 x 10^-4, warmup 700 steps, cosine to 6 x 10^-5; batch, 0.5M tokens per step (256 sequences of 2,048), about 5,000 steps for 2.5B tokens; precision, bf16 autocast with fp32 master weights, clipping at 1.0, FlashAttention through F.scaled_dot_product_attention; logging, loss, grad norm, learning rate, tokens per second and MFU every 10 steps, held-out perplexity every 250, a checkpoint every 500.

The corrected parameter count: with a 32,000-token vocabulary the model has 109.5M parameters (85.0M in the blocks, 24.6M in the tied embedding), not 125M; 124M is GPT-2 small, whose 50,257-token vocabulary and learned positions account for the difference.
The cost: 6ND = 1.64 x 10^18 FLOPs, 1.93 x 10^18 with attention at T = 2,048 (+17%); a few hours on one data-centre GPU, about half a day on a consumer card.

The expected loss: the source's 'about 3.0 nats per token on English web text (perplexity near 20)' kept as an order of magnitude, with two caveats: per-token losses depend on the tokenizer and the corpus and cannot be compared across them; and the Chinchilla fit gives 3.40 at (110M, 2.5B), a statement about Chinchilla's corpus and tokenizer rather than a prediction for this run. To predict this run, fit your own L(N, D) from three or four smaller runs on the same data.

What Module 06's tiny-GPT Decoder lacks for this run: the data pipeline and a loader with state, the schedule, mixed precision, checkpointing, logging and evaluation, which is to say the pipeline (source's point).
The laptop version, Lab 2: 5.8M parameters, 2.46M tokens of TinyStories, about 10 minutes on a CPU with QUICK mode in about 3; the same code structure scaled down about 19,000-fold in compute.
worked_examples: Parameter count: blocks 12 x (4 x 768^2 + 3 x 768 x 2,048 + 2 x 768) = 84,953,088; embedding 32,000 x 768 = 24,576,000; total 109,529,856 plus 768 for the final norm.

Run time: 1.93 x 10^18 FLOPs at 40% of 989 TFLOP/s (H100) -> 1.4 h; at 25% -> 2.2 h; A100 (312 TFLOP/s bf16 dense) at 40% -> 4.3 h, at 25% -> 6.9 h; a consumer GPU with about 165 TFLOP/s dense bf16 at 25-40% -> 8-13 h. Small models reach lower MFU than large ones because their matrices are small.
