sections.title: Mid-training and continued pretraining
sections.purpose: Explain the two cheaper relatives of pretraining (annealing on high-quality data with context extension, and continuing a released base model on a domain) and cost, in full, the case study's decision to continue pretraining its base.
must_cover: Mid-training: a stage between pretraining and post-training on a smaller, higher-quality mixture (more code and mathematics, curated reference text, synthetic textbook-style data, long documents), usually coinciding with the learning-rate decay (the D of WSD); much of the final benchmark quality is won here. Llama 3 annealed on up-sampled high-quality sources at the end of pretraining and used short annealing runs to judge the value of small candidate datasets. It is the cheapest place to add a domain: a few tens of billions of tokens with the domain at a few percent shifts the model without unlearning the rest (source).

Context extension: pretrain at 4k-8k, then train on long documents at 32k-128k with the RoPE base raised or positions interpolated; per-token cost grows with T (attention FLOPs 6LTd), so long context comes late and briefly; staged lengths (Llama 3 extended its context in six stages using about 800B tokens). Methods at concept level: raising the base frequency, position interpolation (Chen et al. 2023, scaling positions by L_train/L_target), NTK-aware scaling and YaRN (Peng et al. 2024). Data: genuinely long documents (books, code repositories, long reports) and synthetic long-context tasks. Evaluate with retrieval from long contexts and long-document questions, and re-run short-context benchmarks to catch regressions. RoPE itself is Module 06's.
Continued pretraining (CPT): start from released base weights and continue next-token training on a domain corpus; s13's pipeline with the initialisation changed.

The source's three rules, expanded: (1) mix in general data (replay), 5-10% or more of a corpus like the base's, more for a larger shift (Ibrahim et al. 2024 found a few percent enough for a weak shift and around a quarter for a strong one such as a new language); (2) a low learning rate, about a tenth of the base's peak, re-warmed briefly and decayed over the planned tokens: a higher re-warmed peak adapts faster and forgets more (Gupta et al. 2023; Ibrahim et al. 2024); the base's optimiser state is rarely released, so Adam's moments start from zero, one more reason for warmup; (3) evaluate general ability throughout, not only domain perplexity.
Forgetting measured: the change in general held-out loss and in a general benchmark battery before and after; Lab 5 measures it at small scale with 0%, 10% and 30% replay and two learning rates.

Tokenizer fit in CPT: a base tokenizer may fragment domain vocabulary (Lab 5 measures 2.34 tokens per word on its domain text against 1.30 on general text, and a tokenizer trained with a fifth domain text brings the domain figure to 1.35); adding tokens means new embedding rows (initialised, for example, as the mean of their sub-token embeddings) that need many steps to learn; usually not worth it for a domain inside the base's languages, and never possible without retraining the embeddings, which is why s4 fixes the tokenizer first.

Whether to do CPT at all: measure the base on the domain first (domain held-out perplexity, a small domain test set); if it already handles the vocabulary and forms, supervised fine-tuning alone (Module 09) is cheaper and enough; CPT moves knowledge and distribution, SFT moves behaviour.

The case study's decision (hypothetical), the one this module costs in full. The gate comes first, before any spend: measure the base on the domain (held-out perplexity on safety-case text against its general held-out perplexity, tokens per word on domain text, a small domain test scored by log-likelihood as in s12). In the case study the gap is large: the base fragments the domain's vocabulary and gives its argument forms low probability, which SFT alone (Module 09) would not fix, so the run is made. The run: 1.8B tokens of safety-engineering text (public accident and incident investigation reports, regulator guidance, published safety cases and the safety-case literature, safety-engineering papers and theses, openly licensed engineering textbooks, each component with its licence in the manifest; copyrighted standards excluded unless licensed) plus 0.2B tokens of general replay (10%); 2B tokens in total; sequence length 8,192; global batch 128 x 8,192 = 1,048,576 tokens, 1,907 steps; peak learning rate 3 x 10^-5 (a tenth of the plan's 3 x 10^-4; a released base's published peak is used where there is one), 100 warmup steps, cosine to 3 x 10^-6; decontaminated against the domain evaluation set; evaluated every 200 steps on domain held-out perplexity, general held-out perplexity and a general battery. The go/no-go rule, fixed in advance: keep the continued-pretraining checkpoint only if domain perplexity falls and the general battery drops by less than a stated margin (for example 1 point). If it is kept, Module 09 starts supervised fine-tuning from it, mixing in general instruction data and training the chat-template tokens the base reserved but never used; if not, Module 09 starts from the instruct release.

The cost, written out (worked example): 1.22 x 10^20 FLOPs by the series' rule, 84.5 GPU-hours at 4 x 10^14 FLOP/s, 10.6 hours on one 8-GPU node, about USD 210 at the series' assumed USD 2.50 per GPU-hour (an assumption, as of 2026): a thousandth of the 2T-token base's 84,500 GPU-hours. The GPU time is the smallest cost of the decision; building and licensing the corpus, the evaluations and the engineers' time dominate it. Memory fits one node without activation checkpointing.
worked_examples: Case-study CPT cost by the series' rule: 6.08 x 10^10 FLOPs per token x 2 x 10^9 tokens = 1.22 x 10^20 FLOPs = 84.5 H100-hours at 4 x 10^14 FLOP/s = 10.6 hours on one 8-GPU node (16 micro-batches of 1 x 8,192 per GPU per step, 19.9 s per step, 2 x 10^9 / 1,048,576 = 1,907 steps); USD 211 at USD 2.50 per GPU-hour (assumed). The source's 6N with N = 9.5B gives 1.14 x 10^20 and 9.9 hours. Memory per GPU with ZeRO-3 over the node: 19.1 (states) + 42.9 (activations) + 5.0 (logits) = 67.0 GB without checkpointing; 27.7 GB with full checkpointing, at a third more compute (s9).

RoPE wavelengths for d_h = 128: the slowest-rotating pair has wavelength 2 pi b^(126/128): 54,410 tokens at base 10^4, 2.56M at 5 x 10^5, 5.06M at 10^6; position interpolation from 8k to 32k multiplies positions by 0.25.
Long-context cost for the case study: per-token training FLOPs 6N_matmul + 6LTd = 6.08 x 10^10 at T = 8,192 and 1.70 x 10^11 at T = 131,072, 2.8 times more per token (s1).

Lab 5's prototype numbers (writers replace them with the executed run): the small base trained inside the lab (1.3M parameters, 819k tokens) has general loss 3.56 and domain loss 7.37 (a uniform guess is 8.32); after 100 steps (205k tokens) at a tenth of the base peak, general loss rose by 1.05 with no replay, 0.26 with 10% replay and 0.13 with 30%, while domain loss fell to 2.45, 2.57 and 2.78; re-warming to the base's full peak drove domain loss to 0.22 but general loss to 9.07 without replay (worse than a uniform guess), and cost only +0.28 with 30% replay (domain loss 0.28).

figures.description: Two routes drawn as stage diagrams with the learning rate traced above each: a lab's route (pretraining: trillions of tokens, warmup then stable; mid-training: tens to hundreds of billions, decay with high-quality data and long context; post-training, Module 09) and an organisation's route (released base -> continued pretraining: billions of tokens, re-warm and decay with replay -> SFT, Module 09). The case study's numbers annotated on the second route (2B tokens: 1.8B domain + 0.2B replay; 1,907 steps; 1.22 x 10^20 FLOPs; 10.6 hours on one 8-GPU node).

Forgetting against adaptation from Lab 5: x = rise in general held-out loss, y = fall in domain held-out loss, one labelled point per run (replay 0%, 10%, 30% at a tenth of the base peak; 0% and 30% at the full peak), with the trade-off frontier drawn; the full-peak, no-replay point drawn off-scale with an arrow and its value.

checks: Why does continued pretraining need a warmup even though the model is already trained? -> The optimiser's moments start from zero (the base's optimiser state is rarely released) and the new data's gradients differ in scale; a full-rate first step can knock the model out of its basin.

When should an organisation skip continued pretraining? -> When the base already handles the domain's vocabulary and forms (measured perplexity and a small domain test), so SFT alone gives the behaviour at far lower cost.
What does replay protect, and what does it cost? -> General ability; it costs a fraction of the token budget and slows domain adaptation slightly.

sections.new_material: Annealing as a data-quality test; context-extension methods and their cost; replay ratios and learning-rate re-warming from the literature; the optimiser-state reset; tokenizer fragmentation in CPT; a concrete hypothetical CPT decision with its gate, data, steps, memory, cost, schedule and go/no-go rule, and what Module 09 starts from; Lab 5's measured trade-off.

what_goes_wrong: Every benchmark number is inflated by an unknown amount -> the evaluation set was in the training data (no decontamination, or a paraphrased copy slipped through) -> decontaminate by n-gram overlap before training, keep the removal list, add a private dated evaluation set, and treat any benchmark you did not decontaminate against as contaminated.

The model recites training passages and misses its scaling-law prediction -> deduplication skipped or done only exactly -> add MinHash-LSH near-duplicate removal and line-level boilerplate removal; check with a memorisation probe on known-duplicated text.

Training loss falls unusually fast while held-out loss stalls -> a shard duplicated many times by a loader or sharding bug -> log tokens per source and per shard; hash shards; compare against the manifest.

Loss stuck near ln V from the first step -> tokenizer mismatch between the data pipeline and the model (or shuffled vocabulary ids) -> decode a batch back to text at the start of every run and store the tokenizer hash in the checkpoint.
The model emits padding or end-of-document tokens and the loss looks good -> padding counted in the loss -> mask padding with ignore_index; with packing there should be no padding at all.
Half the gradients are zero and the run barely learns -> fp16 without loss scaling (underflow) -> use bf16, or dynamic loss scaling, and log the fraction of zero gradients.

A run that was fine at 1B diverges at step 8,000 at 10B -> the learning rate from the small sweep used unchanged at the larger width -> lower the peak for larger models, use muP or a fitted scaling rule, lengthen the warmup, add QK-norm and z-loss.

Loss stalls well above the reference run and attention entropy collapses -> attention-logit growth at a high learning rate (max q.k/sqrt(d_h) in the hundreds) -> QK-norm; a lower peak rate; monitor the maximum attention logit.

A loss spike recurs at the same step after every restart -> a bad batch at that position in the data order -> rewind to a checkpoint about 100 steps before the spike and skip the next few hundred batches; inspect and log the skipped data.

A node failure costs a day of compute -> checkpoints every 5,000 steps (10.4 hours in the case-study plan) -> set the interval with Young's formula from the measured failure rate and write time; checkpoint asynchronously; test restores.

After a restart the loss jumps and the data repeats -> checkpoint saved without the optimiser state or the data-loader position -> save weights, master weights, both moments, scheduler, RNG states and loader position; Lab 2's resume test shows the difference.

Run out of memory at step 1, or MFU far below plan -> activations and fp32 logits not counted, or FSDP gathering weights across slow inter-node links -> do the s8 arithmetic first; checkpoint activations; use fused cross-entropy; shard within nodes (HSDP) or add TP inside the node.

After continued pretraining the model writes good domain text but can no longer follow a format or do simple arithmetic -> domain-only data at a re-warmed high learning rate -> replay 10-30% general data, use about a tenth of the base's peak, evaluate general ability throughout and stop by a go/no-go rule.

The loss is fine and the model is bad -> wrong mixture, a quality classifier that removed the domain you needed, or a tokenizer that fragments it -> evaluate per source and downstream from early in the run; audit what each filter removed; measure tokens per word on the target domain before training.

labs.title: A mini data pipeline: quality filters and MinHash-LSH from scratch
labs.goal: Build the heuristic filters and the near-duplicate detector of s2-s3 on a corpus with known junk and known duplicates, and check MinHash and the LSH S-curve against the theory.
labs.data: TinyStories validation split as one parquet file, 9.99 MB, fetched with huggingface_hub.hf_hub_download('roneneldan/TinyStories', 'data/validation-00000-of-00001-869c898b519ad725.parquet', repo_type='dataset') and read with pandas (21,990 stories); cached for Labs 2, 3 and 5. The first 5,000 stories are the clean documents; junk and duplicates are generated in code from fixed seeds.
steps: Build the corpus with known labels and print its composition: 5,000 clean stories; 150 navigation pages (lines of 6 menu items joined by ' | '); 150 keyword-spam pages (60-120 tokens drawn from BUY, NOW!!!, $$$, #deal, #sale, CHEAP, >>>, ***, 100%, FREE); 150 repeated-line pages (one story sentence repeated 8-15 times); 150 short pages (5-25 words); 200 exact copies of random stories; 600 near-copies with a fraction q of words replaced, q in {0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.08, 0.12, 0.20}: 6,400 documents.

gopher_quality(text) returns the first rule failed (word count 50-100,000; mean word length 3-10; hash and ellipsis ratio <= 0.1; bullet lines <= 90%; ellipsis lines <= 30%; alphabetic words >= 80%; at least 2 of the 8 stop words; duplicate-line fraction <= 0.30; top-2-gram character fraction <= 0.20) or None; print a cross-table of label against rule. Prototype result: all 150 short pages fail on word count; 149 of 150 spam pages on the symbol ratio; navigation pages on non-alphabetic words (107) or word count (43); repeated-line pages mainly on stop words (121) and duplicate lines (25); 3 of 5,000 clean stories removed (2 under 50 words, 1 for ellipsis lines). Also print the statistics for s2's three worked-example documents.

Encoding check on real data: count documents containing mojibake (UTF-8 punctuation mis-decoded as Windows-1252, e.g. 'herâ€”she' for 'her—she'): the prototype found 303 among the first 5,000 stories (1,232 of all 21,990), none caught by any Gopher rule; repair with text.encode('cp1252').decode('utf-8') where the round trip succeeds (97 of 303 in the prototype) and flag the rest, noting that dedicated repair tools exist.

Exact deduplication: lower-case, collapse whitespace, SHA-1, keep the first occurrence; print the number of duplicates found (the prototype found 250, not the 200 inserted: near-copies at q = 0.01 that received no edit are exact copies, and some generated junk coincides).

Shingles and MinHash: 5-word lower-cased shingles; shingle ids by zlib.crc32 (stable across runs, unlike Python's hash()); k = 128 universal hashes h(x) = (a x + b) mod (2^31 - 1) with a, b from a seeded NumPy generator, vectorised (products fit in uint64); time it (under 1 s for 6,400 documents); compare estimated with exact Jaccard on 300 near-copy pairs (prototype: mean absolute error 0.029, maximum 0.13), matching sqrt(J(1 - J)/128).

LSH with b = 16, r = 8: bucket by (band, band bytes); collect candidate pairs (prototype: 750 candidates against 20,476,800 possible pairs, 0.4 s); for the 600 constructed near pairs print the detection rate by true-Jaccard bin next to 1 - (1 - s^8)^16 at the bin centre (prototype: 0.00/0.00 below 0.4, 0.01/0.03 for 0.4-0.5, 0.12/0.13 for 0.5-0.6, 0.41/0.40 for 0.6-0.7, 0.81/0.82 for 0.7-0.8, 0.97/0.99 for 0.8-0.9, 1.00/1.00 above 0.9); plot fig-08-5 with these points.

Verify candidates with exact Jaccard and remove near-duplicates at thresholds 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9 with union-find clusters (keep the lowest index in each cluster); print documents removed, precision and recall against the constructed labels at each threshold (source exercise 2).
Print the pipeline summary (documents in, removed per stage, documents out) and the reason log for five removed documents.
expected_observations: Each kind of junk is caught by the rule designed for it, and almost all clean stories pass; the few that fail show that thresholds tuned for web pages misfire on very short children's stories.
About 6% of the real stories carry mojibake that no quality rule catches; Lab 2's model, trained on them, learns to emit 'â€œ' in its samples: encoding repair is a pipeline stage of its own.
The exact-duplicate count exceeds the 200 inserted, because light edits sometimes change nothing: generator labels are not ground truth.
Measured detection rates follow the S-curve; pairs below J = 0.5 are almost never candidates, so copies with one word in eight changed survive a 5-gram MinHash pass.
LSH looks at about 750 pairs instead of 20.5 million.
extensions: Repeat the LSH step with (b, r) = (32, 4) and (8, 16) and compare candidate counts and recall.

Decontamination: hold out 50 stories as a 'benchmark', insert 10 of them into the corpus with one sentence changed, and count how many a 13-gram overlap test finds; then paraphrase two by hand and test again.
Run gopher_quality on structured technical text, for example ten lines in the form 'Goal G2: The hazard of overpressure of the reactor vessel is acceptably mitigated.', and note which rules misfire.

labs.title: Pretrain a small GPT on TinyStories
labs.goal: Run the whole pipeline of s13 at laptop scale (tokenizer, packing, model, AdamW with warmup-cosine, clipping, logging with throughput and MFU, evaluation, checkpointing and resumption) and save the run's deliverables (s12).
labs.data: The same 9.99 MB TinyStories validation parquet (downloaded if absent, cached after the first time): 21,990 stories, 19.2M characters; a fixed permutation holds out 1,000 stories for validation and trains on the other 20,990.
steps: Settings: QUICK = False (True gives 150 steps, about 3 minutes); SEED = 0; device = 'cuda' if available else 'cpu' (bf16 autocast only on CUDA). Measure the machine's matmul rate (20 products of 1,024 x 1,024 fp32 matrices) and print it in GFLOP/s; it is the 'peak' for MFU (about 600 GFLOP/s on 4 threads of a fast desktop; laptops lower).

Train a byte-level BPE with vocabulary 4,096 and one special token <|endoftext|> on the training stories with the tokenizers library (about 4 s); print the tokens of 'Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily.' (13 tokens, one per word and punctuation mark) and the compression: 3.95 characters per token, 1.29 tokens per word (vocabulary 2,048 gives 3.61 and 1.42).

Pack: encode every story, append the end-of-text id, concatenate into a uint16 array (prototype: about 4.65M training tokens and 0.23M validation tokens); print the padding waste avoided (57% if every story were padded to 512 tokens).

Model: Module 06's decoder with RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU and tied embeddings, d = 256, L = 6, 8 heads, d_ff = 688, context 256, initialisation std 0.02 with residual projections scaled by 1/sqrt(2L); print 5,795,072 parameters (Lab 4's params() reproduces the count from the shape).

Optimiser: AdamW betas (0.9, 0.95), eps 10^-8, weight decay 0.1 on matrices only (two parameter groups; print their sizes); peak 3 x 10^-3, warmup 60 steps (QUICK 30), cosine to 3 x 10^-4 over 600 steps (QUICK 150); batch 16 x 256 = 4,096 tokens; clipping at 1.0.

Training loop on random windows of 257 tokens: every 25 steps print step, tokens seen, loss, grad norm, learning rate, tokens/s and MFU = (6N + 6LTd) x tokens/s / measured matmul rate; every 150 steps print validation loss on 20 fixed batches and the accuracy on the 24-item two-choice cloze set of the next step, scored by summed log-probability; at the midpoint save a checkpoint (model, optimiser, step, torch and NumPy generator states).

The cloze set, 24 two-choice items scored by the summed log-probability of each option (with its leading space) given the context; writers use them verbatim, correct option first. Eighteen that one sentence decides: 'Once upon a time, there was a little girl named' Lily / table; 'She was very happy because she got a new' toy / sad; 'The dog wagged its' tail / book; 'Tom was hungry, so he ate an' apple / car; 'It was raining, so they took an' umbrella / elephant; 'At night, the sky was full of' stars / soup; 'Lily asked, "Can I go to the park?" Mom said, "Yes, you' can / blue; 'The bird flew up into the' sky / spoon; 'Ben fell down and hurt his' knee / cloud; 'They played in the sand at the' beach / book; 'The ice cream was cold and' sweet / angry; 'The little boat floated on the' water / bread; 'He was sad because he lost his' ball / happy; 'The baby was tired, so she went to' sleep / fly; 'The fish swam in the' pond / tree; 'Max wanted to play, but it was time for' bed / sky; 'The car went fast down the' road / cake; 'At the end of the day, the sun went' down / fork. Six that need an earlier sentence: 'Kate lost her red hat in the park. The next day, she went back to the park to look for her' hat / dog; 'Ben had a dog and a cat. The dog liked to bark, and the cat liked to' meow / bark; 'It was a cold winter day. Outside, the ground was covered with' snow / sand; 'Lily was sad because her doll was broken. Then Dad fixed it, and Lily felt' happy / sad; 'Sam loved to swim. Every day after school, he went to the' pool / library; 'The sky was dark and full of clouds. Soon it began to' rain / shine.
After training print total time, final validation loss and perplexity, and a 120-token sample at temperature 0.8 from 'Once upon a time'.

Resume test: load the midpoint checkpoint into a fresh model and optimiser, run 3 steps with the restored generator and print the losses beside those logged at the same steps (equal to about 6 decimal places); repeat with a fresh optimiser (zero moments) and show the losses differ.

Save the final checkpoint (state dict and config) and the tokenizer as the run's deliverable (s12; no later lab reads them, since every lab is self-contained); plot loss against tokens with the learning rate on a second axis.
expected_observations: Loss starts at about 8.34, close to ln 4,096 = 8.32 (a uniform guess), falls below 5 within about 200,000 tokens as frequent words are learned, and reaches a validation loss of about 2.8 (perplexity about 17) after 2.46M tokens; QUICK reaches about 4.0. Validation tracks training because no window repeats. (Prototype: 2.835 full, 4.02 QUICK.)

Throughput: the prototype ran at about 6,800 tokens/s (MFU about 42% of the measured matmul rate) on 4 threads of a desktop CPU when the machine was otherwise idle, and at under half that when other programs competed; a laptop typically manages 3,000-5,000 tokens/s, so the full run takes about 8-14 minutes. MFU is a property of the whole machine, not just the model.
Grad norm is about 6 at step 0, falls below 1 within about 75 steps and settles near 0.5; clipping at 1.0 acts only in the first few dozen steps.

Cloze accuracy moves in steps of about 4 points (one item in 24): the prototype scored 54% at initialisation, 62% after QUICK and 88% after the full run, where the 18 one-sentence items saturated (18 of 18) and the 6 that need an earlier sentence stayed at chance (3 of 6): the noise lesson of s12 in miniature, and a measure of what a 5.8M-parameter model has not learned.
The resumed run matches the logged losses only when the optimiser state and the generator state are both restored.
Full-run samples are story-shaped with frequent grammatical slips ('the sun was too fell full'); QUICK samples are word salad made of story vocabulary.

Replace warmup-cosine with WSD (constant after warmup, linear decay over the last 20%) and compare the final loss and the loss just before the decay starts.

With a GPU (Colab): device = 'cuda', bf16 autocast, d = 512, L = 8, 5,000 steps; compute MFU against the GPU's published dense bf16 peak; then scale towards s13's recipe (source exercise 5's 'run the 125M recipe for an hour').

labs.title: Provoke an instability, then find the fix that works
labs.goal: Reproduce at laptop scale the high-learning-rate instability of s7, diagnose it from logged signals, measure what warmup, clipping, z-loss and QK-norm each contribute, and draw a learning-rate sensitivity curve in the manner of Wortsman et al.
labs.data: The cached TinyStories parquet (10 MB, downloaded if absent); the first 8,000 stories, tokenised with a 4,096-token byte-level BPE trained here in about 4 s on the 20,990 training stories (Lab 2's recipe and split, repeated so the lab runs on its own).
steps: A smaller model for speed: d = 128, L = 4, 4 heads (d_h = 32), d_ff = 352, context 128, batch 16 x 128 = 2,048 tokens, about 1.3M parameters; a qk_norm switch (RMSNorm on q and k per head, before RoPE); a probe that records the largest |q.k|/sqrt(d_h) over the batch on the last step; weight decay 0.1 everywhere.

run(lr, warmup=0, clip=None, z_loss=0.0, qk_norm=False, steps=150) trains from the same seed on the same batches every time; it records per-step cross-entropy, grad norm and mean log Z and returns the final loss (mean of the last 20 steps), the worst loss after step 20, the maximum attention logit, the mean log Z and the maximum grad norm. A run takes 15-40 s on a laptop.
Reference: lr = 3 x 10^-3 with no warmup and no clipping. Prototype: final loss 4.58, max attention logit 34.
Provoke: lr = 3 x 10^-2 with no warmup and no clipping. Prototype: final loss 5.44, max attention logit 897, max grad norm 9. Plot both loss curves.

Apply the textbook fixes cumulatively at lr = 3 x 10^-2 and print a table: + warmup 50 steps (prototype 5.37, logit 627); + clipping at 1.0 (5.46, 1,075); + z-loss 10^-4 (5.43, 1,266). The loss stays about 0.8-0.9 nats above the reference and the logits stay in the hundreds or above.
Add QK-norm on top. Prototype: final loss 4.79, max attention logit 12. The failure was attention-logit growth, the one QK-norm targets.

Learning-rate sensitivity: final loss for lr in {3 x 10^-3, 3 x 10^-2, 10^-1} without any stabiliser and with all four (three new runs; the others are reused); plot final loss against lr on a log axis, two curves. Prototype: bare 4.58, 5.44, 5.32; with all four 4.18, 4.79, 4.80 (max attention logits 7, 12, 17 against 34, 897, 637). Nine runs in all; the prototype took 279 s on a desktop CPU that other jobs were sharing (13-59 s per run).
Print a diagnosis from the logs: the maximum attention logit separates failing runs from healthy ones; grad norm and log Z do not.
expected_observations: At 3 x 10^-2 the loss stalls about 0.9 nats above the reference while the attention logits grow about 25-fold: each softmax has collapsed onto single positions, so attention stops passing useful gradient.

Warmup, clipping and z-loss do not cure this failure, because they target other ones (oversized early steps, gradient spikes, output-logit drift); within a fixed step budget warmup even costs a little. Choosing a fix by mechanism, not by habit, is the lesson.

QK-norm bounds the logits near sqrt(d_h) = 5.7 times the learned gains and recovers most of the gap (prototype: 4.79 against 5.44, with the reference at 4.58); it helps even at the reference rate (4.18 against 4.58), where the logits had already reached 34.

With all four stabilisers the loss is almost the same at 3 x 10^-2 and 10^-1 (4.79 and 4.80 in the prototype) but still 0.6 nats above the best run: stabilisers flatten the sensitivity curve and widen the range of usable learning rates; they do not make a too-high rate optimal.
No NaN appears: at this scale the instability shows as a stall; at large scale the same mechanism produces loss spikes and divergence (s11).
extensions: Log the attention entropy per head every 10 steps for the 3 x 10^-2 run with and without QK-norm and plot it: the collapse is visible before the loss stalls.
Remove weight decay and run 300 steps at 3 x 10^-2 with QK-norm, with and without z-loss; watch the mean log Z.
Repeat the sensitivity sweep at width 256 and see whether the best bare learning rate moves (the muP question of s5).

labs.title: A budget and memory calculator
labs.goal: Write the arithmetic of s1, s5, s8 and s9 as small Python functions (with a preview of s10 and s11), reproduce the module's tables from them, and use them to decide which configurations fit.
labs.data: None: pure arithmetic on the configurations given in the module.
steps: params(L, d, n_h, n_kv, d_ff, V, tied) returns the total and a per-component breakdown; print it for the case study (9,550,729,216), the Llama 3 8B shape (8,030,261,248), the 110M recipe of s13 (109,529,856, plus 768 for the final norm if counted) and Lab 2's model (5,795,072), next to 12Ld^2 for each.

train_flops(N, D, n_embed=0, L=None, T=None, d=None) returns the series' count 6(N - n_embed)D + 6LTdD (the attention term only if L, T and d are given) and the quick 6ND; gpu_time(C, peak, mfu, n_gpus) returns GPU-hours and days. Print the source's five-row budget table at 4 x 10^14 FLOP/s with the source's own arithmetic (6N with N = 9.5B, no attention) and a days column (19.6, 41.2, 309, 0.9, 0.4); the case study under the series' rule (2T tokens: 1.22 x 10^23 FLOPs, 84,465 GPU-hours, 44.0 days on 80 GPUs; continued pretraining on 2B: 1.22 x 10^20 FLOPs, 84.5 GPU-hours, 10.6 hours on 8 GPUs); and the 2T plan at 30%, 40% and 50% of 989 TFLOP/s (59.3, 44.5 and 35.6 days).

chinchilla_loss(N, D), chinchilla_optimum(C) (the 20-tokens-per-parameter point and the fitted law's analytic minimum, Module 07's formula) and equal_loss_payback(N, D). Print the case-study decision of s1 (fitted minimum 15.5B on 1.23T at L = 1.999; 20-tokens point 30.9B on 618B at 2.005; the case study at 2.002; equal-loss optimum 15.0B on 1.18T with a break-even of 7.4 x 10^11 served tokens), then check your answer to e2.
model_states(N, n_d, stage, bytes=(2, 2, 12)) for stage in DP, 1, 2, 3; print the case-study table on 8, 64 and 80 GPUs (8 GPUs: 152.8, 52.5, 35.8, 19.1 GB).

activations(L, d, h_kv, d_ff, T, b, flash=True, ckpt='none' or 'full') and logits_bytes(T, b, V); print 42.9 GB, 3.61 GB and 4.98 GB for the case study at 1 x 8,192, and 155 GB of attention probabilities with flash=False.

fits(config, gpu_gb=80) combining the two; print a table for four configurations: case study, ZeRO-3 on 8 GPUs, no checkpointing (67.0 GB, fits); the same with full checkpointing (27.7 GB); case study, ZeRO-1 on 80 GPUs, no checkpointing (87.5 GB, does not fit); the 110M recipe on one 24 GB GPU with plain AdamW at micro-batch 16 x 2,048 (1.75 + 9.66 + 4.19 = 15.6 GB, fits) and at 32 x 2,048 (29.5 GB, does not: use accumulation).
bubble(p, m) and young_interval(delta, mtbf), with the formulas of s10 and s11 (read next session); print the four bubble cases of s10 and the two checkpoint intervals of s11 (19 minutes; 4.6 hours).
expected_observations: The table reproduces the source's FLOPs and GPU-hours; '16 GPUs for a month' becomes 19.6 days; the series' rule moves the 2T plan from the source's 41 days to 44.0.
Model states, not activations, rule out plain data parallelism for 9.5B; once ZeRO-3 shards over 80 GPUs, activations and logits (48 GB) dwarf the states (1.9 GB).
Checkpointing changes which ZeRO stage fits on 8 x 80 GB: without it only ZeRO-3 fits; with it ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 do too.
Loss differences between compute-optimal and over-trained choices are hundredths of a nat; inference-cost differences are factors.

Plot fig-08-2's iso-FLOP curves for C = 10^20 ... 10^23 with the case-study points.
Add a communication estimate (bytes per GPU per step for DP, ZeRO-3, TP and PP) and reproduce the four layout options of s10 for 80 GPUs.

labs.title: Continued pretraining with and without replay
labs.goal: Train a small base inside the lab, continue its pretraining on a synthetic corpus of safety-case arguments, and measure adaptation and forgetting for different replay ratios and learning rates: the case study's continued pretraining in miniature.
labs.data: No new download: the cached TinyStories parquet (10 MB, downloaded if absent) for general text and for the base's pretraining; the domain corpus generated in code from templates with a fixed seed. The tokenizer and the base are trained inside the lab, so it reads no file written by another lab.
steps: Load the stories with Lab 2's split (a permutation with seed 0 holds out 1,000); train the same 4,096-token byte-level BPE on the 20,990 training stories (about 4 s); declare Lab 2's model class in full (repeated so the lab runs on its own).

Generate the domain corpus: 3,300 safety-case argument documents in a GSN-like textual form from templates (8 systems, each with its environment and three hazards; the first is the case study's own, 'the pressure-relief system' in 'a chemical plant' with 'overpressure of the reactor vessel', 'a relief valve that fails to open' and 'a blocked vent line'; the others are a braking controller, a reactor protection system, a flight control computer, a railway interlocking, a battery management system, a robot arm controller and a ventilator, because a safety-engineering corpus spans industries; causes such as 'a stuck sensor'; mitigations such as 'a hardware watchdog that forces a safe state'; evidence such as 'fault tree analysis'; integrity targets SIL 2/3, ASIL B/D, DAL A/C; lines such as 'Goal G2: The hazard of overpressure of the reactor vessel is acceptably mitigated.' and 'Solution Sn1: Failure modes and effects analysis shows that a hardware watchdog that forces a safe state detects the fault within 50 ms.'). 3,000 for training (about 1.06M tokens), 300 held out (about 105k). Print the first pressure-relief document.

Tokenizer fit: tokens per word on general text against domain text with the base tokenizer (prototype: 1.30 against 2.34); train a second BPE on 12,000 stories plus the 3,000 domain documents (a fifth domain text by characters) and show the domain figure falls (prototype: 1.35, with general text at 1.31); the base cannot use the new tokenizer without retraining its embeddings, which is why the tokenizer is fixed first (source exercise 3, carried here).

The base: d = 128, L = 4, 4 heads, d_ff = 352, context 128, tied embeddings, 1,328,256 parameters (Lab 3's shape without QK-norm); AdamW as in Lab 2, peak 3 x 10^-3 with 30 warmup steps and cosine to 3 x 10^-4, clipping at 1.0, 400 steps of 16 x 128 tokens (819,200 tokens) of general stories; about a minute on a desktop CPU (prototype: 65 s; loss 8.32 at step 0, 3.44 at the end). It stands in for a released base: smaller and shorter-trained than Lab 2's model so that the whole lab fits its runtime. Keep a copy of its state dict for the runs.
Baseline: general validation loss (held-out stories) and domain validation loss of the base on 10 fixed batches each (prototype: 3.56 and 7.37).

Five continued-pretraining runs from the base copy, each 100 steps x 16 x 128 tokens (204,800 tokens), warmup 10 steps, cosine to a tenth of the peak, clipping at 1.0, AdamW as in Lab 2 with fresh moments; each sequence drawn from general text with probability equal to the replay ratio: (a) no replay, peak 3 x 10^-4 (a tenth of the base's); (b) 10% replay, 3 x 10^-4; (c) 30% replay, 3 x 10^-4; (d) no replay, re-warmed to the base's peak 3 x 10^-3; (e) 30% replay, 3 x 10^-3. Print general and domain losses and their changes from the base (prototype: 15-18 s per run).
Plot fig-08-22 (rise in general loss against fall in domain loss, one point per run).
Generate 60 tokens from 'Goal G1:' and from 'Once upon a time' with the base and with runs (a) and (c) to see adaptation and forgetting as text.
expected_observations: The base tokenizer fragments domain words (about 2.3 tokens per word against 1.3), and the base's domain loss starts near 7.4, not far below a uniform guess (ln 4,096 = 8.32), because the base has never seen text like it.

Prototype (the whole lab took 165 s on a desktop CPU, the five runs 85 s): at a tenth of the base peak, general loss rose by 1.05 with no replay, 0.26 with 10% and 0.13 with 30% replay, while domain loss fell from 7.37 to 2.45, 2.57 and 2.78. Replay cuts forgetting four- to eightfold for a small loss of adaptation.

Re-warming to the base's full peak adapts much further in the same 100 steps (domain loss 0.22) but without replay destroys the general model (general loss 9.07, worse than a uniform guess at 8.32); 30% replay at the same peak limits the damage to +0.28 with domain loss 0.28. The learning rate sets how far the model moves and replay how much of the old model it keeps: complements, not substitutes, and which run passes depends on a go/no-go margin fixed before looking.

Generated text shows the trade (prototype samples): the base continues 'Goal G1:' with story text; run (a) slides from 'Once upon a time' into 'Solution' and 'Goal' fragments; run (c) still tells a story from 'Once upon a time', and its 'Goal G1:' continuation mixes goal lines with story words.
extensions: Find the smallest replay ratio that keeps the general-loss rise below 0.1 at the low peak.
Continue run (a) for another 100 steps on general data only and measure how much general ability returns.

Bilingual tokenizer (source exercise 3 as written): save the English and Chinese editions of this module as plain text, train 2,000- and 8,000-token BPEs on 50/50 and 20/80 mixtures, and report characters per token for each language.

exercises.prompt: List four decisions that must be fixed before a pretraining run starts, because changing them later wastes the compute already spent, and one decision that can safely change during the run. Give the reason for each.
exercises.solution_sketch: Fixed: the tokenizer (every token and the embedding table depend on it); the model's shape and size N (the weights are incompatible with any other shape); the data pipeline's filters and deduplication for the data already consumed (tokens trained on cannot be untrained); the schedule's horizon under warmup-cosine (the decay is tied to T; WSD removes this one). Changeable: the mixture for later stages (mid-training is exactly that), the batch size (ramps are common), the checkpoint interval, or the parallel layout (checkpoints can be resharded). Any four of the first kind with reasons earn full marks.

exercises.prompt: For a compute budget C = 10^21 FLOPs, compute the compute-optimal N and D by the 20-tokens-per-parameter rule and the loss predicted by the Chinchilla fit of Module 07, L(N, D) = 1.69 + 406.4/N^0.34 + 410.7/D^0.28. Then compute the loss for a model a quarter as large trained on four times the tokens, and say what the difference buys at inference.
exercises.solution_sketch: C = 6N(20N) = 120N^2, so N = sqrt(10^21/120) = 2.89 x 10^9 and D = 5.77 x 10^10. L = 1.69 + 406.4/N^0.34 + 410.7/D^0.28 = 1.69 + 0.247 + 0.398 = 2.335. Quarter size: N = 7.22 x 10^8, D = 2.31 x 10^11, L = 1.69 + 0.396 + 0.270 = 2.356, worse by 0.02 nats (0.9%). Same training compute, a quarter of the inference FLOPs per token (2N), a quarter of the weight memory. (The fitted law's own minimum is 1.82B on 91.4B tokens at L = 2.329: flat.)

exercises.prompt: A team has 64 H100 GPUs (989 TFLOP/s dense bf16 each, the series' assumed peak) for 30 days and expects 38% MFU. Using the series' FLOP rule (6N_matmul + 6LTd per token, N_matmul excluding the input embedding), how many tokens can it train the case-study model on at T = 8,192 (L = 36, d = 4,096, N = 9.55 x 10^9 of which 0.62 x 10^9 is the input embedding), and how many tokens per parameter is that? How far off is the shortcut 6ND over all parameters, and what goes wrong if the schedule is planned with it?
exercises.solution_sketch: C = 64 x 30 x 86,400 s x 0.38 x 989 x 10^12 = 6.23 x 10^22 FLOPs. Per token: 6 x 8.93 x 10^9 = 5.36 x 10^10 plus 6 x 36 x 8,192 x 4,096 = 7.25 x 10^9, total 6.08 x 10^10. D = 6.23 x 10^22 / 6.08 x 10^10 = 1.03 x 10^12 tokens, 107 per parameter: over-trained relative to Chinchilla, about half the 2T plan. The shortcut 6 x 9.55 x 10^9 = 5.73 x 10^10 per token gives 1.09 x 10^12 tokens (114 per parameter), 6% too many: a cosine schedule planned for 1.09T tokens would not reach its end within the 30 days (about two days short), so the run would stop before its learning rate had decayed.

exercises.prompt: Derive the probability that a pair with Jaccard similarity s becomes an LSH candidate with b bands of r rows. Then, using at most 128 hash functions, find (b, r) such that pairs with J >= 0.85 are caught with probability at least 0.95 and pairs with J <= 0.5 with probability at most 0.05. Which feasible choice uses the fewest hash functions?
exercises.solution_sketch: A band matches with probability s^r (all r MinHash values agree, each with probability s, independently); no band matches with probability (1 - s^r)^b; P = 1 - (1 - s^r)^b. Search: r = 8 works with b = 10 to 13 (b = 10: P(0.85) = 0.958, P(0.5) = 0.038; b = 13: 0.984 and 0.0496); r = 9 works with b = 12 to 14 (b = 12: 0.958/0.023; b = 13: 0.967/0.025; b = 14, k = 126: 0.975/0.027); no other r is feasible within 128 hashes. Fewest hashes: b = 10, r = 8, k = 80. Tightening the lower bound to J <= 0.6 makes the problem infeasible with 128 hashes: the S-curve cannot be that steep.

exercises.prompt: C4's cleaning removed every page containing a curly bracket. Why does this rule remove almost all source code, and what would you do instead for a corpus that should contain code?
exercises.solution_sketch: Curly brackets delimit blocks in most programming languages and appear in JSON, CSS and templating, so nearly every code page contains one; the rule was aimed at JavaScript and boilerplate in web pages. Build code as a separate component from repositories, with its own filters (licence, file type, length, auto-generated and minified files, near-duplicate removal at file level) and mix it in at a chosen weight.

exercises.prompt: A 2T-token run gives a 15B-token mathematics source 3% of its tokens, so the run sees it four times. The team wants to double that weight. Using Muennighoff et al. (2023), say what happens to the value of the extra tokens, and name three other ways to get more mathematics into the model.
exercises.solution_sketch: Doubling the weight means eight epochs, beyond the roughly four over which repeated data is nearly as good as fresh: the extra repetitions are worth much less, and heavy repetition raises memorisation. Alternatives: find or generate more mathematical text (other sources, synthetic problems with checked solutions); raise the weight only in mid-training, whose token count is small, so a higher share adds few repetitions (s14); keep 3% and lean on related sources such as code and papers. Whichever is chosen, measure it with a held-out mathematics loss and a small benchmark.

exercises.prompt: Show that the cross-entropy loss is unchanged when the same constant c is added to every logit, and explain what z-loss adds and why a long bf16 run needs it.
exercises.solution_sketch: softmax(z + c)_j = e^(z_j + c) / sum_i e^(z_i + c) = softmax(z)_j, so the cross-entropy, which depends only on the softmax, is unchanged; nothing in the loss pins the logits' level, which can drift. z-loss adds 10^-4 (log Z)^2, whose gradient 2 x 10^-4 log Z softmax_j pulls log Z towards 0. In bf16 large logits lose precision (spacing 0.125 near 30) and can overflow, so a drifting level eventually destabilises training.

exercises.prompt: Starting from Delta L_opt(B) = Delta L_max / (1 + B_noise/B), derive the number of steps S and tokens D needed to reach a fixed loss as functions of B (in tokens), and show (S/S_min - 1)(D/D_min - 1) = 1. For B_noise = 3M tokens, compute S/S_min and D/D_min at B = 1M and B = 6M tokens.
exercises.solution_sketch: If each step at batch B achieves 1/(1 + B_noise/B) of the best possible progress, the number of steps scales as S = S_min (1 + B_noise/B) (S_min as B -> infinity). Tokens D = S B = S_min (B + B_noise), so D_min = S_min B_noise (as B -> 0) and D/D_min = 1 + B/B_noise. Then (S/S_min - 1)(D/D_min - 1) = (B_noise/B)(B/B_noise) = 1. B = 1M: S/S_min = 4, D/D_min = 1.33. B = 6M: S/S_min = 1.5, D/D_min = 3. The first is data-efficient but slow; the second is fast but burns three times the minimum data.

exercises.prompt: Llama 3 8B's shape (s5): L = 32, d = 4,096, 32 query and 8 KV heads of 128 (h_kv = 1,024), SwiGLU d_ff = 14,336, V = 128,256, untied, 8,030,261,248 parameters. It is trained with bf16 mixed-precision Adam on one node of 8 x 80 GB GPUs with a micro-batch of one 8,192-token sequence per GPU. Compute the model-state memory per GPU under plain data parallelism and ZeRO stages 1, 2 and 3; add the activations (12d + 4h_kv + 6d_ff bytes per token per layer) with and without full activation checkpointing, and the fp32 logits. Which configurations fit in 80 GB, and what differs from the case study in s9?
exercises.solution_sketch: States (N = 8.03 x 10^9): DP 16N = 128.5 GB; ZeRO-1 4N + 12N/8 = 32.1 + 12.0 = 44.2 GB; ZeRO-2 2N + 14N/8 = 16.1 + 14.1 = 30.1 GB; ZeRO-3 16N/8 = 16.1 GB. Activations: 12 x 4,096 + 4 x 1,024 + 6 x 14,336 = 139,264 bytes per token per layer; x 8,192 x 32 = 36.5 GB without checkpointing; with it 2 x 4,096 x 8,192 x 32 = 2.15 GB stored + 1.14 GB for one layer = 3.29 GB. Logits 8,192 x 128,256 x 4 = 4.20 GB. Without checkpointing: DP 169.2, ZeRO-1 84.9, ZeRO-2 70.8, ZeRO-3 56.8 GB, so ZeRO-2 and ZeRO-3 fit; with it: DP 136.0 (never fits), ZeRO-1 51.7, ZeRO-2 37.6, ZeRO-3 23.6 GB. For the case study only ZeRO-3 fits without checkpointing (ZeRO-2 needs 83.7 GB): a model 16% smaller with a narrower FFN moves ZeRO-2 under the line, so whether a stage fits is arithmetic about a model, not a property of the stage.

exercises.prompt: A pipeline-parallel run with GPipe scheduling spends a third of its time idle in the bubble. Name three changes that shrink the bubble and what each costs.
exercises.solution_sketch: (1) More micro-batches per step, by splitting the batch finer or raising the global batch: the idle fraction (p - 1)/(m + p - 1) falls as m grows, but GPipe holds every micro-batch's activations until its backward pass, so switch to 1F1B, which holds at most p; smaller micro-batches also run less efficiently, and a larger global batch may pass the critical batch size (s6). (2) Interleaved stages, v virtual stages per GPU: the bubble falls by a factor v for v times more point-to-point messages. (3) Fewer stages: each GPU then holds more layers, so the memory has to come from ZeRO sharding, activation checkpointing or tensor parallelism instead.

exercises.prompt: Your training loss shows a sawtooth with a period of exactly 1,000 steps that is not in the learning-rate schedule. Give the two most likely causes and how you would confirm each from logs you already have or can add cheaply.
exercises.solution_sketch: (1) The data loader cycles through shards in a fixed order without shuffling across shards, so the loss follows the shard sequence: log the shard id and offset per step and correlate. (2) Code that runs every 1,000 steps changes training state: an evaluation that leaves the model in eval mode or changes the random state, or a checkpoint save that resets the loader: diff the step before and after, and check model.training and the generator state after evaluation and saving. A schedule bug is ruled out by plotting the logged learning rate.

exercises.prompt: A team checkpoints every 5,000 steps because writing a checkpoint takes 2 minutes. Using Young's formula qualitatively, explain why the right interval depends on the failure rate as well as the write time, how it should change when the job moves to a cluster ten times larger (failures scaling with GPU count), and what asynchronous checkpointing changes.
exercises.solution_sketch: The overhead per unit time is delta/tau (writing) plus tau/(2M) (on average half an interval of work is lost per failure): checkpointing less often shrinks the first term and inflates the second, so the optimum balances them at tau* = sqrt(2 delta M), set by both. Ten times the GPUs means a tenth of the mean time between failures: the interval should shrink by sqrt(10), about 3, and even at the optimum the overhead grows by the same factor. A fixed 5,000-step interval ignores both effects. Asynchronous checkpointing shrinks the blocking part of delta to the seconds needed to copy states to host memory, which shortens tau* and cuts the overhead; the failure term then dominates, so measure M.

exercises.prompt: A weight equal to 0.5 is stored in bf16 and receives an update of 1 x 10^-3. What value does it hold afterwards? What about an update of 3 x 10^-3? If it receives 1 x 10^-3 on each of ten steps, what does a bf16 weight hold at the end, and what does the bf16 copy of an fp32 master weight hold? What does this say about storing master weights in bf16?
exercises.solution_sketch: In [0.5, 1) bf16 keeps 7 mantissa bits, so the spacing is 0.5 x 2^-7 = 2^-8 = 0.0039 and half a spacing 0.00195. 0.5 + 0.001 = 0.501 rounds back to 0.5: the update is lost. 0.5 + 0.003 = 0.503 is nearer 0.50390625 than 0.5: the update becomes 0.0039, 30% too large. Ten updates of 0.001 to a bf16 weight are each lost, so it stays at 0.5, although it should have moved by 0.01, two and a half spacings. An fp32 master weight (spacing 2^-24, 6.0 x 10^-8, at 0.5) accumulates them to 0.51, and its bf16 copy is the nearest representable value, 0.51171875, within half a spacing of the truth. Updates below half a spacing vanish and others are distorted, so master weights and the update are kept in fp32 (or bf16 with stochastic rounding or compensated summation).

exercises.prompt: A continued-pretraining run lowers domain perplexity by 20% but raises general held-out loss by 0.15 nats and costs 3 points on a general benchmark battery. Name two changes to the recipe and predict their effect on each of the two numbers.
exercises.solution_sketch: Raise replay (e.g. 10% to 30% general data): general loss rise and benchmark drop shrink, domain gain slightly smaller (Lab 5 prototype: going from 10% to 30% replay cut the general rise from +0.26 to +0.13, while the domain loss ended at 2.78 instead of 2.57). Lower the peak learning rate (or shorten the run): less forgetting, slower domain adaptation. Either way decide by a go/no-go rule fixed in advance; if the general cost cannot be brought within it, skip CPT and rely on SFT.

exercises.prompt: Scaling check and a duplicated shard, at laptop scale (source exercise 5). (a) Run Lab 2 with QUICK = False, logging validation loss on 5 fixed batches every 25 steps (about 10 minutes); fit L(D) = L_inf + a D^-gamma to the first half of the curve (tokens seen against validation loss, with scipy.optimize.curve_fit), extrapolate to the end, and compare with the measured final loss; plot both on log-log axes. (b) Run Lab 2 twice with QUICK = True (about 3 minutes each): once unchanged and once with a 'duplicated shard', drawing 10% of each batch's windows from a fixed 5,000-token slice of the training data. Compare the final validation losses, and the training loss on the duplicated slice against the validation loss, across the two runs.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) A power law fitted on the first 300 steps extrapolates to within a few tenths of a nat of the final loss, but the cosine decay bends the late curve below a pure power law, so the extrapolation tends to be pessimistic; fitting the stable phase of a WSD run is cleaner, and a fit is only a check if it is made before the run ends. (b) The 5,000-token slice is seen about 12 times in a QUICK run; its training loss falls well below the validation loss (memorisation) while the validation loss ends about the same or slightly worse than the clean run, because a tenth of the compute went on re-learning the same text. That pattern in the logs (loss on part of the data falling faster than held-out loss) is the duplicated-shard signature of s11. With a GPU, repeat at s13's scale as the source exercise intended.

quiz.question: A 2B-parameter dense model is trained on 100B tokens. About how many training FLOPs is that?
quiz.explanation: C ≈ 6ND = 6 x 2 x 10^9 x 10^11 = 1.2 x 10^21 by the shortcut (the series' rule, without the input embedding and with attention, moves it by a few percent). 4 x 10^20 is 2ND, the forward pass only; 2.4 x 10^21 doubles the count; 1.2 x 10^20 drops a factor of ten.

quiz.question: In bf16 mixed precision with Adam and fp32 master weights, how many bytes of model state does each parameter need before activations?
quiz.explanation: 2 (bf16 weights) + 2 (bf16 gradients) + 4 (fp32 master) + 4 + 4 (Adam moments) = 16. 12 is the optimiser part alone (master weights and moments); 4 and 8 count only weights and gradients in fp32 or bf16.

quiz.question: Why do LLM pretraining recipes set Adam's beta2 to 0.95 rather than the default 0.999?
options: The second-moment estimate adapts within about 20 steps to a change in gradient scale, avoiding oversized steps
It makes Adam equivalent to SGD with momentum
It removes the need for warmup
quiz.explanation: 1/(1 - beta2) is the memory of the second-moment average: 20 steps at 0.95 against 1,000 at 0.999, so a sudden rise in gradient scale is matched quickly. Memory is unchanged; Adam remains adaptive; warmup is still used.

quiz.question: MinHash with k = 128 hash functions estimates a pair's Jaccard similarity of 0.8. What is the standard error of the estimate?
quiz.explanation: Each hash agrees with probability J, so the estimate is a mean of 128 Bernoulli variables: SE = sqrt(J(1 - J)/k) = sqrt(0.16/128) = 0.035. 0.16 is the variance of one hash, not the error of the mean; the other options divide by k without the square root.

quiz.question: With LSH banding of b = 16 bands and r = 8 rows, about how likely is a pair with Jaccard similarity 0.5 to become a candidate?
quiz.explanation: P = 1 - (1 - 0.5^8)^16 = 1 - (0.9961)^16 = 0.061. 0.4% is one band's probability 0.5^8; 50% confuses it with s; 94% is the probability at s = 0.8.

quiz.question: Under ZeRO stage 2 with N parameters on N_d GPUs (16 bytes per parameter in total), how much model-state memory does each GPU hold?
quiz.explanation: Stage 2 shards gradients (2 bytes) and optimiser states (12 bytes) and keeps the bf16 weights (2 bytes) whole. 4N + 12N/N_d is stage 1, 16N/N_d stage 3, 16N plain data parallelism.

quiz.question: A GPipe pipeline has p = 4 stages and m = 12 micro-batches. What fraction of the time is each stage idle?
quiz.explanation: Idle fraction (p - 1)/(m + p - 1) = 3/15 = 20%. 25% is (p - 1)/m, the bubble relative to ideal compute rather than to total time; 33% and 8% come from other mistaken formulas.

quiz.question: Which statement about bf16 and fp16 is correct?
options: bf16 has fp32's exponent range and needs no loss scaling, but fewer mantissa bits than fp16
bf16 has more mantissa bits than fp16, so it is more precise
fp16 has a larger range than bf16
Both need dynamic loss scaling to train LLMs
quiz.explanation: bf16 is 1/8/7 bits, fp16 1/5/10: bf16 trades precision for fp32's range, so small gradients do not underflow. fp16's range ends at 65,504 and about 6 x 10^-8; only fp16 needs loss scaling.

quiz.question: Full activation checkpointing (store each layer's input, recompute the layer in the backward pass) raises training compute by about how much?
quiz.explanation: The forward pass, 2N of the 6N FLOPs per token, is repeated: 8N/6N = 1.33. Recomputing does cost compute, and only the forward pass is repeated, not the backward.

quiz.question: Why is tensor parallelism normally confined to the GPUs of one node?
options: It all-reduces activations in every layer, which needs the bandwidth of intra-node links
It cannot be combined with data parallelism
quiz.explanation: Megatron-style TP needs two all-reduces per layer forward and two backward; for the case study at TP = 2 that is 9.7 GB per micro-batch, 21 ms over NVLink but 0.19 s over InfiniBand. It composes with DP and PP and computes the same function.

quiz.question: A continued-pretraining run on domain text only raises the general held-out loss sharply. What should you change first?
options: Mix in general replay data and lower the peak learning rate
Raise the learning rate to finish sooner
Train longer on the domain text
quiz.explanation: Replay and a low peak are the two levers against forgetting (Lab 5 prototype at a tenth of the peak: no replay +1.05, 30% replay +0.13; re-warmed to the full peak without replay +5.5). A higher rate, longer domain-only training and no warmup all increase forgetting.

quiz.question: On a 500-item benchmark, checkpoint A scores 41% and checkpoint B 44%. What can you conclude?
options: The difference is within noise: each score has a standard error of about 2.2 points
A is better because it is earlier
Nothing can ever be concluded from benchmarks
quiz.explanation: SE = sqrt(0.4 x 0.6/500) = 0.022, a 95% interval of about +/- 4.3 points for each; a 3-point gap is not resolved. Larger test sets or averaging across tasks and checkpoints resolve smaller gaps.

papers.citation: Penedo, G., Kydlíček, H., Ben Allal, L., Lozhkov, A., Mitchell, M., Raffel, C., von Werra, L., Wolf, T. "The FineWeb datasets: Decanting the web for the finest text data at scale." NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks Track, 2024.
papers.why: The best-documented public web pipeline: every stage of s2-s4 with an ablation behind it, including the negative results (global deduplication) that recipes usually omit.
papers.read: Read the introduction, the sections on text extraction, base filtering, deduplication (including the per-snapshot finding) and the FineWeb-Edu annotation and classifier. Skim the custom heuristic filters and the comparison with other datasets. Skip the appendices.
questions: Why did the authors extract text from WARC files with trafilatura instead of using the WET text, and how did they show that it mattered?
What went wrong when they deduplicated across all crawl snapshots at once, and what did they do instead? Why might global deduplication favour older, lower-quality text?
How was the educational-quality classifier built (annotator, scale, number of annotated samples, model) and what threshold produced FineWeb-Edu?
What size of model and how many tokens did they use for their data ablations, and what does that imply about how data decisions are tested?

papers.citation: Rajbhandari, S., Rasley, J., Ruwase, O., He, Y. "ZeRO: Memory optimizations toward training trillion parameter models." SC20: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis, 2020.
papers.why: The source of the 16-bytes-per-parameter accounting and of the three sharding stages that s8 and s9 derive and that FSDP implements.
papers.read: Read the introduction with its memory figure, the analysis of where the memory goes (model states and residual states), the description of the three ZeRO-DP stages, and the communication analysis. Skim ZeRO-R. Skip the implementation and evaluation sections.
questions: Reproduce the paper's per-GPU memory for a 7.5B-parameter model on 64 GPUs under the baseline and the three stages (120, 31.4, 16.6 and 1.9 GB).
Why does sharding the parameters cost only 1.5 times data parallelism's communication rather than more?
What are 'residual states', and which techniques in this module address each of them?

papers.citation: Wortsman, M. et al. "Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities." ICLR, 2024 (arXiv 2023).
papers.why: Shows that the instabilities of large runs can be reproduced and fixed in small models at high learning rates: the method Lab 3 copies, and the evidence behind QK-norm, z-loss and the AdamW epsilon advice.
papers.read: Read the introduction, the sections on attention-logit growth with qk-layernorm and on output-logit divergence with z-loss, and the definition of learning-rate sensitivity. Skim the section on other interventions (warmup, independent weight decay, muParam, the AdamW epsilon). Skip the appendices.
questions: What is learning-rate sensitivity and why is it a more useful summary than the best loss achieved?
What evidence links attention-logit growth to divergence, and how does qk-layernorm change the sensitivity curve? Compare with what Lab 3 measured.
Why does z-loss fix output-logit divergence, and what happens to the logits without it?
What do the authors find about AdamW's epsilon as models grow, and what do they recommend?

widgets.name: compute-budget-planner
widgets.teaching_point: Training compute follows from the configuration and D (the series' rule: 6ND without the input embedding, plus attention), calendar time from GPUs x peak x MFU, and at a fixed budget the predicted loss is flat near the optimum, so a smaller model trained on more tokens costs little loss and saves inference.
controls: slider: parameters N, 10^8 to 10^12, log scale (default 9.551 x 10^9)
slider: training tokens D, 10^9 to 10^14, log scale (default 2 x 10^12), with a live readout of D/N
select: GPU, A100 80GB (312 TFLOP/s dense bf16), H100 SXM 80GB (989), H200 141GB (989), Custom (number input for peak TFLOP/s); default H100 SXM
number: GPU count, 1 to 100,000 (default 80)
slider: MFU 10%-60% in 1% steps (default 40%)

checkbox: count FLOPs by the series' rule (Module 06), 6(N - Ve) + 6LTd per token, with number inputs for the input-embedding parameters Ve = V x d (default 622,854,144), L (default 36), T (default 8,192) and width d (default 4,096); on by default. Off, C is the shortcut 6ND, labelled 'quick estimate'.

number: price per GPU-hour in USD, empty by default with the placeholder 2.50 (the series' assumed H100 price, as of 2026); the cost readout appears only when a price is typed and is labelled as an assumption
buttons: 'Set D to 20 tokens per parameter for this budget' and 'Set N, D to the fitted law's minimum for this budget' (both keep C6 = 6ND fixed)
displays: readouts: C in FLOPs (scientific notation), GPU-hours, calendar days (and months above 60 days) on the chosen GPU count, tokens per parameter, predicted loss L(N, D), forward FLOPs per token (2(N - Ve) under the series' rule, or 2N labelled 'quick, about 7% high'), and cost if a price was given

plot: the iso-FLOP curve L(N) at the current budget in Chinchilla's accounting, C6 = 6ND, N on a log axis from 10^7 to 10^13 clipped to D = C6/(6N) >= 10^8, with the current point, the 20-tokens-per-parameter point and the fitted law's minimum marked and labelled with their (N, D, L); the region outside the fit's range (N outside 7 x 10^7 to 1.6 x 10^10 or D outside 5 x 10^9 to 5 x 10^11) shaded and captioned 'extrapolation'; a footnote: 'Chinchilla counted 6ND over all parameters, so the curve, the optimum and the payback use 6ND; the cost readouts use the series' rule'

panel 'over-training payback': the model at the fitted minimum that reaches the same predicted loss as the current (N, D), its training FLOPs C', and the served-token break-even S* = (6ND - C')/(2(N' - N)); text instead when the current model is larger than that optimum ('this model costs more to train and to serve than the optimum at equal loss')
widgets.defaults: The case study: N = 9.551 x 10^9, D = 2 x 10^12, H100 SXM, 80 GPUs, MFU 40%, series' rule on (Ve = 622,854,144, L = 36, T = 8,192, d = 4,096). Readouts: C = 1.216 x 10^23 FLOPs, 85,405 GPU-hours, 44.5 days (at 0.40 x 989 TFLOP/s; the text's 44.0 days uses the rounded 4 x 10^14 FLOP/s), 209 tokens per parameter, L = 2.002, forward 1.79 x 10^10 FLOPs per token. Unticking the rule gives the quick 6ND: 1.146 x 10^23 FLOPs, 41.9 days. On the iso-FLOP curve (C = 1.146 x 10^23 by 6ND) the case study sits left of the fitted minimum (N' = 15.5B, D' = 1.23T, L = 1.999) and the 20-tokens-per-parameter point (30.9B, 618B, L = 2.005): all three within 0.007 nats. Payback panel: equal-loss optimum 15.0B on 1.18T, C' = 1.065 x 10^23, break-even 7.4 x 10^11 served tokens.
widgets.spec: Constants from Module 07, shown to the reader as the fitted law with its numbers, L = 1.69 + 406.4/N^0.34 + 410.7/D^0.28 (in code E = 1.69, A = 406.4, Bc = 410.7, alpha = 0.34, beta = 0.28; 'Bc' because B is the batch in this series). Training FLOPs: with the rule on, C = [6(N - Ve) + 6LTd] x D, Ve clamped to at most N/2; off, C = 6ND. GPU-hours = C/(peak x 10^12 x MFU)/3600; days = GPU-hours/count/24. L(N, D) = E + A N^-alpha + Bc D^-beta. Chinchilla's own accounting C6 = 6ND is used for the iso-FLOP curve, the 20-tokens point, the fitted minimum, the buttons and the payback panel. 20-tokens point at fixed C6: N20 = sqrt(C6/120), D20 = 20 N20. Fitted minimum at fixed C6: G = (alpha A/(beta Bc))^(1/(alpha + beta)) = 1.3447; N* = G (C6/6)^(beta/(alpha + beta)); D* = (C6/6)/N*. Iso-FLOP curve: L(N, C6/(6N)) sampled at 200 log-spaced N. Equal-loss optimum: bisect on C' over [10^15, 10^28] (60 iterations on log C') until L(N*(C'), D*(C')) equals the current L to 10^-6; N' = N*(C'); break-even S* = (C6 - C')/(2(N' - N)) if N < N', else show the dominated message. Edge cases: clamp inputs to slider ranges; format numbers with three significant figures and thin spaces; never show a cost unless a price was entered; never print a dollar sign (write 'USD'). Vanilla JS with an SVG plot; responsive to 400 px width; light and dark themes.

widgets.name: memory-planner
widgets.teaching_point: Model states (16 bytes per parameter) are what ZeRO shards; activations and logits are what checkpointing, micro-batch size and tensor parallelism control; whether a run fits is arithmetic.
controls: slider: layers L, 2-128 (default 36)
slider: width d, 256-16,384 in steps of 128 (default 4,096)
number: query heads n_h (default 32) and KV heads n_kv (default 8); head dimension shown as d/n_h
number: FFN width d_ff (default 15,360), with the ratio d_ff/d shown
number: vocabulary V (default 152,064); checkbox tied embeddings (default off)
slider: sequence length T, 512-131,072 in powers of two (default 8,192)
slider: micro-batch per GPU b, 1-32 (default 1)
number: sharding / data-parallel degree N_d, 1-1,024 (default 8)
select: tensor-parallel degree t, 1, 2, 4, 8 (default 1), with sequence parallelism assumed
select: precision scheme, 'bf16 + fp32 master + Adam (16 B/param)' (default), 'with fp32 gradient buffers (18 B/param)', '8-bit Adam states (10 B/param)'
select: activation checkpointing, none (default), selective (recompute attention scores), full
checkbox: FlashAttention (default on)
select: GPU memory, 24, 40, 80, 141, 192 GB (default 80)
displays: readouts: total parameters N computed from the shape; activation bytes per token per layer; extra compute from checkpointing (0%, the selective figure 2LTd/(6N + 6LTd), or 33%); state bytes per parameter

four stacked bars, one per strategy (DP, ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2, ZeRO-3): segments for weights, gradients, optimiser states (master weights and moments), activations, logits; a horizontal line at the GPU memory; bars above it hatched where they exceed it and labelled 'does not fit'; GB values as labels and on hover

a line of text per strategy with the communication per optimiser step in GB per GPU: DP, ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 about 2 x 2N/t bytes (gradient reduce-scatter and all-gather); ZeRO-3 about 3 x 2N/t bytes per micro-batch
widgets.defaults: The case study on one 8-GPU node: L = 36, d = 4,096, 32/8 heads, d_ff = 15,360, V = 152,064 untied (N = 9,550,729,216), T = 8,192, b = 1, N_d = 8, t = 1, 16 B/param, no checkpointing, FlashAttention on, 80 GB. Bars: DP 200.7 GB, ZeRO-1 100.4, ZeRO-2 83.7, ZeRO-3 67.0: only ZeRO-3 fits. Switching to full checkpointing gives 161.4, 61.1, 44.4, 27.7: three fit. Turning FlashAttention off adds 155 GB of attention probabilities to every bar.
widgets.spec: d_h = d/n_h (round and warn if n_h does not divide d; warn if n_kv does not divide n_h); h_kv = n_kv d_h. N = L (d n_h d_h + 2 d h_kv + n_h d_h d + 3 d d_ff + 2d) + V d (x2 if untied) + d. Per-GPU parameters P = N/t. State bytes (w, g, o) = (2, 2, 12), (2, 4, 12) or (2, 2, 6); k = w + g + o. DP: k P; ZeRO-1: (w + g) P + o P/N_d; ZeRO-2: w P + (g + o) P/N_d; ZeRO-3: k P/N_d; split each into weight, gradient and optimiser segments accordingly. Activations per token per layer A = (12d + 4h_kv + 6d_ff)/t bytes; none: A b T L; full: 2d b T L/t + A b T; selective: as none. Without FlashAttention add 2 n_h T^2 b L/t bytes unless checkpointing is selective or full. Logits: b T V x 4/t bytes. GB = 10^9 bytes. Bars taller than 3 times the GPU line are drawn broken with the value printed. Large values in TB above 1,000 GB. Vanilla JS with SVG; responsive to 400 px; light and dark themes; colour-blind-safe segment colours with a legend.

RUNNING CASE STUDY (hypothetical, never anyone's plan or product; Module 07 introduces it). An engineering team adapts an open-weight bilingual English-Chinese model of about 9.5B parameters, released as base and instruct checkpoints, to draft and check safety-case arguments for the pressure-relief system of a reactor vessel. Use that name and that domain only (not 'safety-assurance arguments'; a hazard log, not a HARA). Configuration, identical in Modules 07-10: L = 36, d = 4,096, 32 query heads and 8 KV heads of 128, SwiGLU d_ff = 15,360, V = 152,064 (byte-level BPE), untied embeddings, RMSNorm pre-norm, no biases; this module adds the base's pretraining details, RoPE base 500,000 and pretraining context 8,192. Exactly 9,550,729,216 parameters (per layer 230,694,912: attention 41,943,040, FFN 188,743,680, norms 8,192; blocks 8,305,016,832; 622,854,144 per embedding table; final norm 4,096); N_matmul = N - Vd = 8,927,875,072; bf16 weights 19.10 GB. The module uses the case study twice. (1) How such a base is made: the 2T-token plan (about 209 tokens per parameter) on 80 H100s, global batch 480 x 8,192 = 3,932,160 tokens, 508,626 steps, AdamW (0.9, 0.95, 1e-8, wd 0.1), peak 3e-4, 2,000 warmup steps, cosine to 3e-5, bf16 with fp32 master weights, clip 1.0, z-loss 1e-4, HSDP (shard within node, replicate across 10 nodes): 1.22 x 10^23 FLOPs by the series' rule, 84,465 GPU-hours at 4 x 10^14 FLOP/s, 44.0 days, 7.47 s per step. The team never runs it; present it as how a base like theirs is made. (2) The team's own decision, costed in s14: continued pretraining on 1.8B domain + 0.2B replay tokens, 1,907 steps of 1,048,576 tokens, peak 3e-5, one 8-GPU node with ZeRO-3 and no activation checkpointing (67.0 GB per GPU): 1.22 x 10^20 FLOPs, 84.5 GPU-hours, 10.6 hours, about USD 210 at the assumed USD 2.50 per GPU-hour; gated by baselines and a go/no-go rule fixed in advance. In the case study the baselines show a domain gap and the run is made; Module 09 starts SFT from the kept checkpoint (from the instruct release if the rule fails) and Module 10 serves the merged, quantised model. Use 9.5B when quoting the source's table (its rounding) and 9.55B when computing from the configuration; say once in s1 that the two differ by 0.5%. The serving workload (Module 07): 2,000 requests a day of 4,000 input tokens (a 3,000-token stable prefix plus 1,000 tokens of hazard-log entries and the request) and 2,000 output tokens, 12M tokens a day; this module uses it only for the over-training payback in s1.

FLOP AND MEMORY RULE (Module 06 owns it; state it once, in s1, and say which count each figure uses). Forward cost per token 2N_matmul plus 4Ldt at context position t, which averages to 2LdT over a causal sequence of length T; training three times the forward. Case study: forward 1.79 x 10^10 per token; training 5.36 x 10^10 + 6LTd (7.25 x 10^9 at T = 8,192, +13.5%) = 6.08 x 10^10. 6N over all parameters (5.73 x 10^10) appears only labelled as a quick estimate (7% high on the weight term, 6% low overall at 8k). Memory and Chinchilla's N use all parameters. Lab 2's model and the s13 recipe tie their embeddings, so 6N is already their weight term. Chinchilla's own accounting (6ND over all parameters) is kept for the fit's iso-FLOP curves, optimum and payback.

SHARED CONSTANTS (every writer uses these, so parallel parts agree; hardware figures are assumptions, labelled where used). H100 SXM dense bf16 peak 989 TFLOP/s, 3.35 TB/s, 80 GB; sustained 4 x 10^14 FLOP/s (40% MFU), as in Modules 07 and 09, for the source table and the case study; 0.40 x 989 TFLOP/s only in the widget and where the text says 'at the exact peak' (85,405 GPU-hours and 44.5 days for the 2T plan); A100 312 TFLOP/s; NVLink about 450 GB/s per direction per GPU within an 8-GPU node; inter-node about 50 GB/s per GPU (400 Gb/s).
